item.title: Infleqtion Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Infleqtion, ticker I-N-F-Q. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Infleqtion released the numbers on Monday, November sixteenth, twenty twenty-six, after the close, and held its conference call at four thirty in the afternoon Eastern Time. On the call were Marcus Kupferschmidt, head of investor relations and strategic finance; Matt Kinsella, chief executive officer; Pranav Gokhale, chief technology officer and general manager of quantum computing; and Ilan Hart, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Investing.com transcript of that call, the company's earnings release furnished with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company's quarterly report on Form ten-Q, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's move around the release. I will cover the results against expectations, the maintained outlook, management's main points, notable analyst questions from the transcript, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. Infleqtion reported third-quarter revenue of nine point one million dollars, up twenty-five percent from a year earlier. The company called it a record quarter and said all of that revenue was organic and entirely from quantum operations. Revenue for the first nine months of twenty twenty-six was thirty-two point six million dollars, up fifty-seven percent. That growth came with a much wider loss, a miss against published Wall Street estimates, and a maintained full-year twenty twenty-six revenue outlook of at least forty-five point one million dollars. The company also said it had delivered a key technical milestone ahead of schedule: thirty entangled logical qubits working together in a single computation on its Scale system, spelled S-q-a-l-e, using only eighty physical qubits.

On the comparison with expectations, the sources do not all use the same figures, so I will keep them separate and will not invent a single official consensus. The company's statements show revenue of nine million one hundred forty-nine thousand dollars, which management rounded to nine point one million dollars. TipRanks put the consensus revenue estimate at eleven point zero three million dollars and listed the result as a miss of about one point nine million dollars. MarketBeat put the revenue estimate lower, at ten point seven five million dollars, against an actual figure it listed as nine point one five million dollars. Either way, the published estimates I found were looking for more than the company delivered.

The earnings comparison has the same kind of split. The company reported a G.A.A.P. net loss of nineteen point seven million dollars, or nine cents a share, compared with a loss of six point two million dollars, or thirty-eight cents a share, a year earlier. The per-share loss narrowed even as the dollar loss widened, because the share count rose sharply after the company went public earlier this year. Weighted average shares were about two hundred twenty-five point two million this quarter, versus about sixteen point four million a year earlier. TipRanks and MarketBeat both put the consensus at a loss of five cents a share, and both listed a reported figure of an eight-cent loss. MarketBeat also listed G.A.A.P. earnings as a loss of nine cents, matching the company's statements. The company published a non-G.A.A.P. net loss of seventeen point six million dollars, but it did not give a non-G.A.A.P. loss per share. The official G.A.A.P. loss was nine cents a share, and several data services compared a figure near eight or nine cents with a consensus loss of five cents.

The wider dollar loss does not depend on whose estimate you use. G.A.A.P. operating loss was thirty-four point five million dollars, compared with six point seven million dollars a year earlier. Non-G.A.A.P. operating loss was twenty-two point seven million dollars, compared with five point nine million dollars. Hart said the increases primarily reflect investment in headcount and technology development, as well as the incremental cost of operating as a public company, and that the G.A.A.P. figure also reflects higher stock-based compensation. Stock-based compensation in the quarter was ten point nine million dollars, versus about eight hundred thousand dollars a year earlier.

Let me walk through the financials with that context. The mix inside the nine point one million dollars of revenue shifted in a way that matters. Product revenue fell to two point seven million dollars from five point two million dollars a year earlier. Service revenue rose to six point five million dollars from two point one million dollars. Government customers accounted for eighty-nine percent of third-quarter revenue, up from seventy-four percent a year earlier. About eighty-five percent of the quarter's revenue, or seven point eight million dollars, came from the United States. The ten-Q also shows a very high customer concentration. One customer, labeled Customer A, accounted for eighty-one percent of third-quarter revenue, up from forty-four percent a year earlier, and the same customer represented eighty percent of accounts receivable at quarter end.

Gross profit turned negative. The company recorded a gross loss of one point one million dollars, compared with gross profit of three point seven million dollars a year earlier. Total cost of revenue was ten point three million dollars, above the quarter's revenue, versus three point six million dollars a year earlier. Stock-based compensation inside cost of revenue was two point two million dollars, so non-G.A.A.P. cost of revenue was eight point one million dollars. Hart said the sequential decline in revenue and the associated gross-margin pressure reflected the timing of revenue recognition on a government program following an expansion award, as well as lower margins on the final stages of another contract as it concluded. He said the magnitude of that impact was specific to the third quarter, and that the company expects revenue and gross margin to improve in the fourth quarter.

Operating expenses rose sharply. Research and development was eleven point five million dollars, versus four point eight million dollars a year earlier. Selling, general, and administrative expense was twenty-two point zero million dollars, versus six point zero million dollars. Below the operating line, two items narrowed the net loss. The company recorded an unrealized gain of nine point seven million dollars on an equity investment in a privately held company,. Interest income was five point three million dollars, versus seven hundred eighty thousand dollars a year earlier. Those two items are why the net loss of nineteen point seven million dollars is a good deal smaller than the operating loss. They are real this quarter, but the equity-investment gain is marked to a private-company price change, and interest income is a function of the cash pile, not of selling quantum systems at a profit.

For the first nine months of twenty twenty-six, revenue was thirty-two point six million dollars, versus twenty point eight million dollars a year earlier. The nine-month G.A.A.P. operating loss was ninety-seven point four million dollars, and the nine-month net loss was seventy-four point one million dollars, or thirty-nine cents a share, versus a loss of one dollar and thirty-four cents a share a year earlier.

Cash use rose as well. Hart said cash used in operations in the third quarter was sixteen point three million dollars, and capital expenditures were five point two million dollars, compared with six million dollars and one hundred thousand dollars, respectively, a year earlier. He said the increased investment primarily supported computing headcount and expanded facilities and labs. The company ended the quarter with five hundred sixty million dollars in cash, cash equivalents, and available-for-sale securities, and no debt. That balance was down twenty-two million dollars from the prior quarter and included a twenty-eight million dollar temporary working-capital benefit from payroll taxes collected on stock-option exercises. Hart said the company is maintaining its twenty twenty-six guidance for a modest uptick in cash burn.

The most important contracted-demand figure on the call was remaining performance obligations, or R.P.O. Hart told an analyst that overall R.P.O. was fifty-one point two million dollars, up from twenty-one million dollars in the second quarter. The ten-Q breaks that down by timing. As of September thirtieth, the company expected to recognize ten point nine million dollars of that amount in the remainder of twenty twenty-six, thirty-six point one million dollars in twenty twenty-seven, and four point two million dollars in twenty twenty-eight. Kinsella said there had been growth in both computing and sensing, that compute had been particularly strong, and that the company also expects good growth in R.P.O. in the fourth quarter. He said, quote, I’m feeling really bullish about the way things are shaping up for compute in twenty twenty-seven, end quote.

Now to guidance. The company maintained its twenty twenty-six revenue outlook. The press release said at least forty-five point one million dollars. On the call, Kinsella said the company was maintaining full-year revenue guidance of approximately forty-five point one million dollars. Management did not issue a formal fourth-quarter revenue range, but the math implied by the maintained full-year figure and the thirty-two point six million dollars already recorded in the first nine months is a fourth quarter of about twelve point five million dollars. The company did not give formal earnings, margin, or twenty twenty-seven revenue guidance.

Hart also gave a brief update on a Department of Commerce transaction announced in the second quarter. He said the company expects to complete the definitive agreement process later this year, and that under the current structure the amount, up to one hundred million dollars, is expected to be recorded as a financing transaction, with final treatment depending on the definitive agreement and the applicable accounting review. In the question-and-answer session, Kinsella said the company was getting closer to getting that deal inked and did not signal a change in timing.

Kinsella used the technical milestone to define the quarter. He said that in May he had described the first quarter in one word, momentum, and that in August the word for the second quarter was acceleration. For the third quarter, he said, the word is execution, specifically technical execution. The company had committed to demonstrating thirty logical qubits by the end of twenty twenty-six, and it delivered ahead of schedule. He said, quote, Logical qubits are the keys to the kingdom for useful quantum computing, end quote.

Gokhale explained what that demonstration actually was. He said all thirty logical qubits worked together in a single computation. The company had aimed for fewer than ten physical qubits per logical qubit and ended up with fewer than three. He said that efficiency reflects an A.I.-driven advance that reduced the number of physical gates needed for logical entanglement. Infleqtion's approach, he said, intentionally converts hard-to-identify errors into atom loss, because a missing atom tells the software exactly where a problem occurred.

The signature demonstration, he said, ran an algorithm on thirty logical qubits using about one thousand physical operations, which he called one Kilo-Quop. Circuit-level fidelity after those operations was twenty-one percent, versus a random-guessing success rate of just two hundredths of one percent. When the company error-corrected for atom-loss events, he said, it boosted system yield by a factor of thirty-six while reducing application-level fidelity by a factor of three. The company also prepared thirty logical qubits in what he called a Tesseract error-correction code, with a distance of four, meaning it can be used to correct any single physical error. He said a paper with the technical details would be released within the next few weeks.

The next official milestone is one hundred logical qubits capable of one million reliable operations, or one Mega-Quop, in twenty twenty-eight, and a longer-term roadmap toward one thousand logical qubits in twenty thirty. Gokhale said the company now expects to reach Mega-Quop capability with as few as two thousand physical qubits, a significant improvement in efficiency relative to prior estimates. That system, he said, will integrate continuous atom reloading and repeated error correction so the machine can replenish atoms and keep correcting errors during long computations. Kinsella tied customer deployments and the jump in remaining performance obligations to growing confidence that compute revenue will grow strongly in twenty twenty-seven and will represent a meaningfully larger share of total revenue.

On the commercial computing side, management pointed to several named items. In Japan, the company's quantum processing unit now powers what they described as the country's first operational full-stack neutral atom quantum computer, at the Institute for Molecular Science, under Japan's Quantum Moonshot program. The company already has a deployed system at the United Kingdom's National Quantum Computing Centre. At the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park, Gokhale said the company is finalizing site readiness as it prepares to deliver a quantum processing unit in twenty twenty-seven. In energy, he said a customer, Eaton, is working on grid contingency analysis and outage planning. In finance, he said a leading global financial institution, which he did not name, ran tens of thousands of shots of a thirty-logical-qubit circuit on the Scale system in the third quarter. The company also announced collaborations with NVIDIA, Cisco, and Riverlane.

Sensing was the other half of the business update. The company's Ticker clock, spelled T-i-q-k-e-r, demonstrated sustained operation aboard a U.S. Navy support vessel, the R.V. Merlin, at sea. NASA expanded a quantum gravity contract by twenty million dollars, bringing the cumulative value to forty million dollars, for work with the Jet Propulsion Laboratory that Kinsella said aims to fly the world's first quantum gravity sensor in space, with work expected to continue through twenty twenty-seven. In October, the United Kingdom government awarded an approximately twelve million dollar contract to advance the company's Quantum Spectrum direction-finding technology toward a deployable product. Kinsella said a Quantum Spectrum atom-based antenna can be as small as a sugar cube, versus conventional antenna arrays that can be as big as a football field, and that the system receives entirely passively.

Kinsella closed the prepared remarks by saying that as computing systems begin solving commercially relevant problems and the sensing business grows, the company expects revenue to grow faster than operating costs, which is how it will build operating leverage over time. That is a forward-looking claim, not a result this quarter. This quarter, costs and losses widened by much more than revenue grew.

Now to the question-and-answer session.

Jesse Sobelson of B.T.I.G. asked how Infleqtion's mix might evolve between full-stack system deliveries and cloud or software access. Kinsella said that if you had asked him five years ago, he would have thought that by twenty twenty-six the vast majority of commercial quantum activity would be taking place in the cloud. In reality, he said, it has been the exact opposite, and the market is almost entirely driven by system sales. His current mental model is that system sales will be a big part of the mix for a while, with cloud rising as a percentage over time, and that customers will want machines on their premises early on before shifting more toward cloud consumption. On a follow-up about remaining performance obligations, he said both computing and sensing had contributed, with compute particularly strong.

Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities asked what the company had learned getting to thirty logical qubits that gives it confidence in the jump to one hundred. Gokhale said getting to thirty validated key building blocks for one hundred as well, notably the ability to pick up qubits and move them around during a computation, which is why the physical-to-logical ratio is so efficient, and the ability to maintain good performance of the underlying physical gates. To get to one hundred logical qubits, he said, the company will need error-correction codes with a greater distance than the distance-four results already shown, and it will need to reload atoms as they are lost. Ellis then asked how customer conversations had evolved. Kinsella said the company had already started to invest more in compute in the third quarter, because conversations had increased globally and become more specific about applications.

Adrienne Colby, asking for Atif Malik at Citi, asked about the timing of the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park delivery and the mix of compute versus sensing in twenty twenty-seven. Kinsella said the plan is to deliver the system to the park by the end of twenty twenty-seven, and that the company will book that revenue in twenty twenty-seven. For modeling purposes, he said, you can book that ten million dollars as revenue next year, and that this will start to take compute up as a percentage of revenue in twenty twenty-seven compared with twenty twenty-six. Hart agreed. On a follow-up about where the company needs to invest, Kinsella pointed to manufacturing, saying Infleqtion needs to be able to manufacture not only sensing products but computers in greater numbers than in the past.

Ella Dolchinsky of Morgan Stanley asked about the comment that customer engagements are shifting to co-development. Gokhale said a lot of recent interest has come from buyers realizing that the cost of running something on a quantum computer can be one hundred or one thousand times lower than their initial estimates, thanks to the reconfigurability of neutral atoms, and that materials, batteries, solar cells, and catalysts are among the earliest expected applications.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt asked whether a forthcoming paper would include a two-qubit gate error rate. Gokhale said the company prefers to measure success at the level of the entire circuit, but that running about one thousand operations at a net fidelity of twenty-one percent implies a per-gate success rate of about ninety-nine point eight five percent, averaged across many types of gates. McPeake asked whether the Mega-Quop machine would support universal gates. Gokhale said yes.

Tyler Anderson of Craig-Hallum, asking for Richard Shannon, wanted to know whether contract manufacturers were a priority for the one-hundred-logical-qubit machine or for a later machine. Kinsella said the company is looking at potential contract manufacturers first for some of its sensing products, and that the timing for computers is still an internal decision. Kingsley Crane of Canaccord Genuity asked whether political crosscurrents and the recent election had changed the timeline of government awards, including the Department of Commerce transaction. Kinsella said no, and that the company was getting closer to the finish line on that deal. Crane also asked about Intel's acquisition of Classiq. Gokhale said Infleqtion's own combination of hardware and software, after the twenty twenty-two acquisition of Super.tech, was being validated by that kind of deal, and that the bulk of the company's software attention is on deep co-design for neutral atoms on Superstat, spelled Superstaq.

Quinn Bolton of Needham and Company closed with a technical exchange worth translating into plain language. He asked whether a factory-level fidelity of ninety-nine point eight five percent implied a logical error rate of roughly ten to the minus three, and whether the Mega-Quop machine would need something like ten to the minus six. Gokhale said that was effectively the right way to think about it, and that getting from ten to the minus three to ten to the minus six is not a one-thousand-times-harder problem, because quantum error correction becomes more powerful as physical qubits are added. Bolton then asked whether the thirty-logical-qubit demonstration involved many live rounds of error correction. Gokhale said those results used a single round, and that the next step toward one hundred logical qubits and one Mega-Quop is to do many rounds. The milestone is real, but it is not yet the multi-round error correction the twenty twenty-eight machine will require.

The stock's move around the report needs a careful timestamp. The company released results after the close on Monday, November sixteenth, and held the call at four thirty Eastern Time. Investing.com said shares fell six point eight four percent in regular trading to seven dollars and ninety cents, then rose two point five three percent after hours to eight dollars and ten cents. That regular-session decline happened before the results were out, so it should not be read as the market's reaction to the earnings themselves. The after-hours bounce is the immediate move after the release, and even then the shares were still below the prior close of eight dollars and forty-eight cents that Investing.com cited. Investing.com also said the stock had dropped eighteen percent over the prior seven days.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether the fourth quarter actually delivers the reversal management described. The maintained full-year outlook implies a fourth-quarter revenue figure around twelve point five million dollars, and management said both revenue and gross margin should improve after a timing-driven third quarter.

Second, conversion of the fifty-one point two million dollars of remaining performance obligations, and whether that balance keeps growing in the fourth quarter the way Kinsella said he expects. Thirty-six point one million dollars of the current R.P.O. is slated for twenty twenty-seven, but R.P.O. is not the same thing as recognized revenue, and a large share of current revenue already comes from a single customer and from government programs.

Third, the computing mix in twenty twenty-seven. Management is asking investors to believe that compute becomes a meaningfully larger share of the business next year, and Kinsella pointed to about ten million dollars of revenue from the Illinois park system as a modeling input, with delivery planned by the end of twenty twenty-seven.

Fourth, the path from a thirty-logical-qubit, single-round demonstration to a one-hundred-logical-qubit, Mega-Quop machine in twenty twenty-eight. Gokhale said key building blocks have been de-risked, and that multiple rounds of error correction, atom reloading, and systems engineering are the work ahead.

Fifth, cash use and operating leverage. The company has five hundred sixty million dollars of cash and securities and no debt, a long runway at the current quarterly operating cash use of sixteen point three million dollars, but that cash figure includes a twenty-eight million dollar temporary payroll-tax benefit, and both operating losses and capital spending are rising. The leverage thesis is that revenue will grow faster than operating costs. This quarter does not yet show it.

Sixth, the Department of Commerce transaction of up to one hundred million dollars. Management still expects a definitive agreement later this year and currently expects to record it as financing, but it is not closed.

Let me close with a short recap. Infleqtion reported record third-quarter revenue of nine point one million dollars, up twenty-five percent year over year, but below the published consensus estimates I found, which were in a range of about ten point eight million to eleven point zero million dollars. The official G.A.A.P. loss was nine cents a share. The dollar net loss widened to nineteen point seven million dollars, and the G.A.A.P. operating loss widened to thirty-four point five million dollars. Gross profit turned into a one point one million dollar loss, which management blamed on the timing of two government programs and said should reverse in the fourth quarter. The company maintained its full-year revenue outlook of at least forty-five point one million dollars, pointed to fifty-one point two million dollars of remaining performance obligations, and said it had delivered thirty logical qubits ahead of schedule. It ended the quarter with five hundred sixty million dollars of cash and securities and no debt. The follow-through to watch is whether the fourth quarter restores revenue and gross margin, whether that backlog converts into twenty twenty-seven computing revenue, and whether the technical milestone starts to look like a path to operating leverage rather than another reason to spend more.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-infleqtion-q3-2026-revenue-rises-25-as-loss-widens-93CH-5031191

Author: Infleqtion
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Infleqtion, ticker I-N-F-Q. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. Infleqtion released the numbers on Monday, November sixteenth, twenty twenty-six, after the close, and held its conference call at four thirty in the afternoon Eastern Time. On the call were Marcus Kupferschmidt, head of investor relations and strategic finance; Matt Kinsella, chief executive officer; Pranav Gokhale, chief technology officer and general manager of quantum computing; and Ilan Hart, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Investing.com transcript of that call, the company's earnings release furnished with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company's quarterly report on Form ten-Q, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's move around the release. I will cover the results against expectations, the maintained outlook, management's main points, notable analyst questions from the transcript, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. Infleqtion reported third-quarter revenue of nine point one million dollars, up twenty-five percent from a year earlier. The company called it a record quarter and said all of that revenue was organic and entirely from quantum operations. Revenue for the first nine months of twenty twenty-six was thirty-two point six million dollars, up fifty-seven percent. That growth came with a much wider loss, a miss against published Wall Street estimates, and a maintained full-year twenty twenty-six revenue outlook of at least forty-five point one million dollars. The company also said it had delivered a key technical milestone ahead of schedule: thirty entangled logical qubits working together in a single computation on its Scale system, spelled S-q-a-l-e, using only eighty physical qubits.

On the comparison with expectations, the sources do not all use the same figures, so I will keep them separate and will not invent a single official consensus. The company's statements show revenue of nine million one hundred forty-nine thousand dollars, which management rounded to nine point one million dollars. TipRanks put the consensus revenue estimate at eleven point zero three million dollars and listed the result as a miss of about one point nine million dollars. MarketBeat put the revenue estimate lower, at ten point seven five million dollars, against an actual figure it listed as nine point one five million dollars. Either way, the published estimates I found were looking for more than the company delivered.

The earnings comparison has the same kind of split. The company reported a G.A.A.P. net loss of nineteen point seven million dollars, or nine cents a share, compared with a loss of six point two million dollars, or thirty-eight cents a share, a year earlier. The per-share loss narrowed even as the dollar loss widened, because the share count rose sharply after the company went public earlier this year. Weighted average shares were about two hundred twenty-five point two million this quarter, versus about sixteen point four million a year earlier. TipRanks and MarketBeat both put the consensus at a loss of five cents a share, and both listed a reported figure of an eight-cent loss. MarketBeat also listed G.A.A.P. earnings as a loss of nine cents, matching the company's statements. The company published a non-G.A.A.P. net loss of seventeen point six million dollars, but it did not give a non-G.A.A.P. loss per share. The official G.A.A.P. loss was nine cents a share, and several data services compared a figure near eight or nine cents with a consensus loss of five cents.

The wider dollar loss does not depend on whose estimate you use. G.A.A.P. operating loss was thirty-four point five million dollars, compared with six point seven million dollars a year earlier. Non-G.A.A.P. operating loss was twenty-two point seven million dollars, compared with five point nine million dollars. Hart said the increases primarily reflect investment in headcount and technology development, as well as the incremental cost of operating as a public company, and that the G.A.A.P. figure also reflects higher stock-based compensation. Stock-based compensation in the quarter was ten point nine million dollars, versus about eight hundred thousand dollars a year earlier.

Let me walk through the financials with that context. The mix inside the nine point one million dollars of revenue shifted in a way that matters. Product revenue fell to two point seven million dollars from five point two million dollars a year earlier. Service revenue rose to six point five million dollars from two point one million dollars. Government customers accounted for eighty-nine percent of third-quarter revenue, up from seventy-four percent a year earlier. About eighty-five percent of the quarter's revenue, or seven point eight million dollars, came from the United States. The ten-Q also shows a very high customer concentration. One customer, labeled Customer A, accounted for eighty-one percent of third-quarter revenue, up from forty-four percent a year earlier, and the same customer represented eighty percent of accounts receivable at quarter end.

Gross profit turned negative. The company recorded a gross loss of one point one million dollars, compared with gross profit of three point seven million dollars a year earlier. Total cost of revenue was ten point three million dollars, above the quarter's revenue, versus three point six million dollars a year earlier. Stock-based compensation inside cost of revenue was two point two million dollars, so non-G.A.A.P. cost of revenue was eight point one million dollars. Hart said the sequential decline in revenue and the associated gross-margin pressure reflected the timing of revenue recognition on a government program following an expansion award, as well as lower margins on the final stages of another contract as it concluded. He said the magnitude of that impact was specific to the third quarter, and that the company expects revenue and gross margin to improve in the fourth quarter.

Operating expenses rose sharply. Research and development was eleven point five million dollars, versus four point eight million dollars a year earlier. Selling, general, and administrative expense was twenty-two point zero million dollars, versus six point zero million dollars. Below the operating line, two items narrowed the net loss. The company recorded an unrealized gain of nine point seven million dollars on an equity investment in a privately held company,. Interest income was five point three million dollars, versus seven hundred eighty thousand dollars a year earlier. Those two items are why the net loss of nineteen point seven million dollars is a good deal smaller than the operating loss. They are real this quarter, but the equity-investment gain is marked to a private-company price change, and interest income is a function of the cash pile, not of selling quantum systems at a profit.

For the first nine months of twenty twenty-six, revenue was thirty-two point six million dollars, versus twenty point eight million dollars a year earlier. The nine-month G.A.A.P. operating loss was ninety-seven point four million dollars, and the nine-month net loss was seventy-four point one million dollars, or thirty-nine cents a share, versus a loss of one dollar and thirty-four cents a share a year earlier.

Cash use rose as well. Hart said cash used in operations in the third quarter was sixteen point three million dollars, and capital expenditures were five point two million dollars, compared with six million dollars and one hundred thousand dollars, respectively, a year earlier. He said the increased investment primarily supported computing headcount and expanded facilities and labs. The company ended the quarter with five hundred sixty million dollars in cash, cash equivalents, and available-for-sale securities, and no debt. That balance was down twenty-two million dollars from the prior quarter and included a twenty-eight million dollar temporary working-capital benefit from payroll taxes collected on stock-option exercises. Hart said the company is maintaining its twenty twenty-six guidance for a modest uptick in cash burn.

The most important contracted-demand figure on the call was remaining performance obligations, or R.P.O. Hart told an analyst that overall R.P.O. was fifty-one point two million dollars, up from twenty-one million dollars in the second quarter. The ten-Q breaks that down by timing. As of September thirtieth, the company expected to recognize ten point nine million dollars of that amount in the remainder of twenty twenty-six, thirty-six point one million dollars in twenty twenty-seven, and four point two million dollars in twenty twenty-eight. Kinsella said there had been growth in both computing and sensing, that compute had been particularly strong, and that the company also expects good growth in R.P.O. in the fourth quarter. He said, quote, I’m feeling really bullish about the way things are shaping up for compute in twenty twenty-seven, end quote.

Now to guidance. The company maintained its twenty twenty-six revenue outlook. The press release said at least forty-five point one million dollars. On the call, Kinsella said the company was maintaining full-year revenue guidance of approximately forty-five point one million dollars. Management did not issue a formal fourth-quarter revenue range, but the math implied by the maintained full-year figure and the thirty-two point six million dollars already recorded in the first nine months is a fourth quarter of about twelve point five million dollars. The company did not give formal earnings, margin, or twenty twenty-seven revenue guidance.

Hart also gave a brief update on a Department of Commerce transaction announced in the second quarter. He said the company expects to complete the definitive agreement process later this year, and that under the current structure the amount, up to one hundred million dollars, is expected to be recorded as a financing transaction, with final treatment depending on the definitive agreement and the applicable accounting review. In the question-and-answer session, Kinsella said the company was getting closer to getting that deal inked and did not signal a change in timing.

Kinsella used the technical milestone to define the quarter. He said that in May he had described the first quarter in one word, momentum, and that in August the word for the second quarter was acceleration. For the third quarter, he said, the word is execution, specifically technical execution. The company had committed to demonstrating thirty logical qubits by the end of twenty twenty-six, and it delivered ahead of schedule. He said, quote, Logical qubits are the keys to the kingdom for useful quantum computing, end quote.

Gokhale explained what that demonstration actually was. He said all thirty logical qubits worked together in a single computation. The company had aimed for fewer than ten physical qubits per logical qubit and ended up with fewer than three. He said that efficiency reflects an A.I.-driven advance that reduced the number of physical gates needed for logical entanglement. Infleqtion's approach, he said, intentionally converts hard-to-identify errors into atom loss, because a missing atom tells the software exactly where a problem occurred.

The signature demonstration, he said, ran an algorithm on thirty logical qubits using about one thousand physical operations, which he called one Kilo-Quop. Circuit-level fidelity after those operations was twenty-one percent, versus a random-guessing success rate of just two hundredths of one percent. When the company error-corrected for atom-loss events, he said, it boosted system yield by a factor of thirty-six while reducing application-level fidelity by a factor of three. The company also prepared thirty logical qubits in what he called a Tesseract error-correction code, with a distance of four, meaning it can be used to correct any single physical error. He said a paper with the technical details would be released within the next few weeks.

The next official milestone is one hundred logical qubits capable of one million reliable operations, or one Mega-Quop, in twenty twenty-eight, and a longer-term roadmap toward one thousand logical qubits in twenty thirty. Gokhale said the company now expects to reach Mega-Quop capability with as few as two thousand physical qubits, a significant improvement in efficiency relative to prior estimates. That system, he said, will integrate continuous atom reloading and repeated error correction so the machine can replenish atoms and keep correcting errors during long computations. Kinsella tied customer deployments and the jump in remaining performance obligations to growing confidence that compute revenue will grow strongly in twenty twenty-seven and will represent a meaningfully larger share of total revenue.

On the commercial computing side, management pointed to several named items. In Japan, the company's quantum processing unit now powers what they described as the country's first operational full-stack neutral atom quantum computer, at the Institute for Molecular Science, under Japan's Quantum Moonshot program. The company already has a deployed system at the United Kingdom's National Quantum Computing Centre. At the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park, Gokhale said the company is finalizing site readiness as it prepares to deliver a quantum processing unit in twenty twenty-seven. In energy, he said a customer, Eaton, is working on grid contingency analysis and outage planning. In finance, he said a leading global financial institution, which he did not name, ran tens of thousands of shots of a thirty-logical-qubit circuit on the Scale system in the third quarter. The company also announced collaborations with NVIDIA, Cisco, and Riverlane.

Sensing was the other half of the business update. The company's Ticker clock, spelled T-i-q-k-e-r, demonstrated sustained operation aboard a U.S. Navy support vessel, the R.V. Merlin, at sea. NASA expanded a quantum gravity contract by twenty million dollars, bringing the cumulative value to forty million dollars, for work with the Jet Propulsion Laboratory that Kinsella said aims to fly the world's first quantum gravity sensor in space, with work expected to continue through twenty twenty-seven. In October, the United Kingdom government awarded an approximately twelve million dollar contract to advance the company's Quantum Spectrum direction-finding technology toward a deployable product. Kinsella said a Quantum Spectrum atom-based antenna can be as small as a sugar cube, versus conventional antenna arrays that can be as big as a football field, and that the system receives entirely passively.

Kinsella closed the prepared remarks by saying that as computing systems begin solving commercially relevant problems and the sensing business grows, the company expects revenue to grow faster than operating costs, which is how it will build operating leverage over time. That is a forward-looking claim, not a result this quarter. This quarter, costs and losses widened by much more than revenue grew.

Now to the question-and-answer session.

Jesse Sobelson of B.T.I.G. asked how Infleqtion's mix might evolve between full-stack system deliveries and cloud or software access. Kinsella said that if you had asked him five years ago, he would have thought that by twenty twenty-six the vast majority of commercial quantum activity would be taking place in the cloud. In reality, he said, it has been the exact opposite, and the market is almost entirely driven by system sales. His current mental model is that system sales will be a big part of the mix for a while, with cloud rising as a percentage over time, and that customers will want machines on their premises early on before shifting more toward cloud consumption. On a follow-up about remaining performance obligations, he said both computing and sensing had contributed, with compute particularly strong.

Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities asked what the company had learned getting to thirty logical qubits that gives it confidence in the jump to one hundred. Gokhale said getting to thirty validated key building blocks for one hundred as well, notably the ability to pick up qubits and move them around during a computation, which is why the physical-to-logical ratio is so efficient, and the ability to maintain good performance of the underlying physical gates. To get to one hundred logical qubits, he said, the company will need error-correction codes with a greater distance than the distance-four results already shown, and it will need to reload atoms as they are lost. Ellis then asked how customer conversations had evolved. Kinsella said the company had already started to invest more in compute in the third quarter, because conversations had increased globally and become more specific about applications.

Adrienne Colby, asking for Atif Malik at Citi, asked about the timing of the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park delivery and the mix of compute versus sensing in twenty twenty-seven. Kinsella said the plan is to deliver the system to the park by the end of twenty twenty-seven, and that the company will book that revenue in twenty twenty-seven. For modeling purposes, he said, you can book that ten million dollars as revenue next year, and that this will start to take compute up as a percentage of revenue in twenty twenty-seven compared with twenty twenty-six. Hart agreed. On a follow-up about where the company needs to invest, Kinsella pointed to manufacturing, saying Infleqtion needs to be able to manufacture not only sensing products but computers in greater numbers than in the past.

Ella Dolchinsky of Morgan Stanley asked about the comment that customer engagements are shifting to co-development. Gokhale said a lot of recent interest has come from buyers realizing that the cost of running something on a quantum computer can be one hundred or one thousand times lower than their initial estimates, thanks to the reconfigurability of neutral atoms, and that materials, batteries, solar cells, and catalysts are among the earliest expected applications.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt asked whether a forthcoming paper would include a two-qubit gate error rate. Gokhale said the company prefers to measure success at the level of the entire circuit, but that running about one thousand operations at a net fidelity of twenty-one percent implies a per-gate success rate of about ninety-nine point eight five percent, averaged across many types of gates. McPeake asked whether the Mega-Quop machine would support universal gates. Gokhale said yes.

Tyler Anderson of Craig-Hallum, asking for Richard Shannon, wanted to know whether contract manufacturers were a priority for the one-hundred-logical-qubit machine or for a later machine. Kinsella said the company is looking at potential contract manufacturers first for some of its sensing products, and that the timing for computers is still an internal decision. Kingsley Crane of Canaccord Genuity asked whether political crosscurrents and the recent election had changed the timeline of government awards, including the Department of Commerce transaction. Kinsella said no, and that the company was getting closer to the finish line on that deal. Crane also asked about Intel's acquisition of Classiq. Gokhale said Infleqtion's own combination of hardware and software, after the twenty twenty-two acquisition of Super.tech, was being validated by that kind of deal, and that the bulk of the company's software attention is on deep co-design for neutral atoms on Superstat, spelled Superstaq.

Quinn Bolton of Needham and Company closed with a technical exchange worth translating into plain language. He asked whether a factory-level fidelity of ninety-nine point eight five percent implied a logical error rate of roughly ten to the minus three, and whether the Mega-Quop machine would need something like ten to the minus six. Gokhale said that was effectively the right way to think about it, and that getting from ten to the minus three to ten to the minus six is not a one-thousand-times-harder problem, because quantum error correction becomes more powerful as physical qubits are added. Bolton then asked whether the thirty-logical-qubit demonstration involved many live rounds of error correction. Gokhale said those results used a single round, and that the next step toward one hundred logical qubits and one Mega-Quop is to do many rounds. The milestone is real, but it is not yet the multi-round error correction the twenty twenty-eight machine will require.

The stock's move around the report needs a careful timestamp. The company released results after the close on Monday, November sixteenth, and held the call at four thirty Eastern Time. Investing.com said shares fell six point eight four percent in regular trading to seven dollars and ninety cents, then rose two point five three percent after hours to eight dollars and ten cents. That regular-session decline happened before the results were out, so it should not be read as the market's reaction to the earnings themselves. The after-hours bounce is the immediate move after the release, and even then the shares were still below the prior close of eight dollars and forty-eight cents that Investing.com cited. Investing.com also said the stock had dropped eighteen percent over the prior seven days.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether the fourth quarter actually delivers the reversal management described. The maintained full-year outlook implies a fourth-quarter revenue figure around twelve point five million dollars, and management said both revenue and gross margin should improve after a timing-driven third quarter.

Second, conversion of the fifty-one point two million dollars of remaining performance obligations, and whether that balance keeps growing in the fourth quarter the way Kinsella said he expects. Thirty-six point one million dollars of the current R.P.O. is slated for twenty twenty-seven, but R.P.O. is not the same thing as recognized revenue, and a large share of current revenue already comes from a single customer and from government programs.

Third, the computing mix in twenty twenty-seven. Management is asking investors to believe that compute becomes a meaningfully larger share of the business next year, and Kinsella pointed to about ten million dollars of revenue from the Illinois park system as a modeling input, with delivery planned by the end of twenty twenty-seven.

Fourth, the path from a thirty-logical-qubit, single-round demonstration to a one-hundred-logical-qubit, Mega-Quop machine in twenty twenty-eight. Gokhale said key building blocks have been de-risked, and that multiple rounds of error correction, atom reloading, and systems engineering are the work ahead.

Fifth, cash use and operating leverage. The company has five hundred sixty million dollars of cash and securities and no debt, a long runway at the current quarterly operating cash use of sixteen point three million dollars, but that cash figure includes a twenty-eight million dollar temporary payroll-tax benefit, and both operating losses and capital spending are rising. The leverage thesis is that revenue will grow faster than operating costs. This quarter does not yet show it.

Sixth, the Department of Commerce transaction of up to one hundred million dollars. Management still expects a definitive agreement later this year and currently expects to record it as financing, but it is not closed.

Let me close with a short recap. Infleqtion reported record third-quarter revenue of nine point one million dollars, up twenty-five percent year over year, but below the published consensus estimates I found, which were in a range of about ten point eight million to eleven point zero million dollars. The official G.A.A.P. loss was nine cents a share. The dollar net loss widened to nineteen point seven million dollars, and the G.A.A.P. operating loss widened to thirty-four point five million dollars. Gross profit turned into a one point one million dollar loss, which management blamed on the timing of two government programs and said should reverse in the fourth quarter. The company maintained its full-year revenue outlook of at least forty-five point one million dollars, pointed to fifty-one point two million dollars of remaining performance obligations, and said it had delivered thirty logical qubits ahead of schedule. It ended the quarter with five hundred sixty million dollars of cash and securities and no debt. The follow-through to watch is whether the fourth quarter restores revenue and gross margin, whether that backlog converts into twenty twenty-seven computing revenue, and whether the technical milestone starts to look like a path to operating leverage rather than another reason to spend more.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-infleqtion-q3-2026-revenue-rises-25-as-loss-widens-93CH-5031191

item.title: US Air Force advances restartable hypersonic rocket engine to power high-speed weapons
item.description:
US Air Force advances restartable hypersonic rocket engine to power high-speed weapons. From Interesting Engineering, by Kaif Shaikh, published November 13th, 2026.

Here's the headline in one sentence: the Air Force Research Laboratory, known as AFRL, has put more money behind a rocket engine called Draper, built by the American propulsion company Ursa Major. The engine is designed for hypersonic applications, and it has already powered two flights of an experimental missile demonstrator. Let's walk through what was announced, what makes this engine different, and just as importantly, what this news does not mean.

First, the money. AFRL has exercised a contract option worth ten point nine million dollars to keep developing the Draper engine. An option, in government contracting terms, is a pre-negotiated extension that the customer can choose to trigger. In other words, the Air Force liked what it saw and decided to keep going. This award builds on a larger, twenty-eight point six million dollar AFRL contract that was announced back in May of 2025. Under that original deal, Ursa Major was tasked with maturing the engine and integrating it into a flight demonstrator.

That demonstrator is called the Affordable Rapid Missile Demonstrator, or ARMD for short. And it uses Draper as its propulsion system. AFRL and Ursa Major first announced a flight demonstration in March of 2026, and they reported that the vehicle reached supersonic speeds. Then, roughly forty-five days later, a follow-on flight took place. That second flight expanded the demonstrator's flight envelope, meaning it pushed into new combinations of speed, altitude, and maneuvering, and it tested how the engine performed and how well it could be controlled during different phases of flight.

Now, here's an important caveat that the article is careful to make. These flights are a real development milestone, but they are not a publicly confirmed hypersonic flight. AFRL described the March demonstration as supersonic. Supersonic means faster than the speed of sound. Hypersonic is a much higher bar, generally considered to be five times the speed of sound or more. So the program's broader objective is to develop propulsion technology for future high-speed weapons and test vehicles, but what has been publicly shown so far is supersonic flight.

So why is the Air Force interested in this particular engine? It comes down to a trade-off that has shaped missile design for decades: solid rockets versus liquid rockets.

Solid rocket motors are the workhorses of most missiles. Their big advantage is that they're simple and ready to go. The fuel is cast into the motor, it sits there, and when you need it, you light it. The downside is that once a solid motor is ignited, it generally burns at a predetermined rate until it's done. You can't really turn it down, and you can't turn it off and back on.

Liquid rocket engines, on the other hand, offer much more control. You can adjust the flow of propellant, which changes the thrust. But many liquid engines use cryogenic propellants, like liquid oxygen, which have to be kept extremely cold. That means specialized temperature-controlled storage and fueling right before launch, which is not very practical for a weapon that might need to sit on a shelf, or under an aircraft wing, ready at a moment's notice.

Draper is designed to get the best of both worlds. According to Ursa Major, the engine produces about four thousand pounds of thrust, and it runs on hydrogen peroxide and kerosene in what the company calls a closed catalyst cycle. The key point is that both of those propellants can be stored at room temperature. The company says they can remain stored for years. That means a vehicle could be prepared for launch without first having to load or condition its fuel, much like a solid rocket.

But unlike a solid rocket, Draper is throttleable, meaning its thrust can be adjusted up or down during flight. And according to the company, it can also restart multiple times. Picture a missile that can burn hard to accelerate, then throttle back or shut down to coast, and then reignite later in its flight to sprint or maneuver. That kind of flexibility gives designers far more control over a vehicle's flight profile than a conventional solid motor allows.

Why does that matter? The article points to two uses. One is hypersonic test vehicles. The military needs targets and test articles that can reproduce the changing speed and maneuverability of advanced threats, the kind of hypersonic weapons that adversaries are developing. An engine that can throttle and restart can mimic those behaviors more realistically. The second use is future tactical weapons that need more control over their propulsion during flight.

The ARMD program itself is also about speed of development, not just speed of flight. It's intended to demonstrate how quickly a new propulsion system and a missile-like vehicle can be developed, integrated, and flown. Ursa Major says the first ARMD flight came about eight months after the contract began. And the second flight, coming about a month and a half after the first, showed a rapid turnaround between missions. In a defense world where programs can take a decade or more, that pace is a big part of the pitch.

Draper is also central to Ursa Major's broader hypersonics business. In February of 2026, the company unveiled a missile system called HAVOC, which it describes as a medium-range hypersonic weapon powered by the Draper engine. The company says HAVOC can throttle and restart during different phases of flight, and that it's designed for potential launch from aircraft, ships, and ground-based systems. The article is careful to note that these are company-stated design capabilities. They are not evidence that the weapon has entered operational service.

Ursa Major has another engine in its stable as well, called Hadley. Hadley is also a liquid rocket engine, and it has powered Stratolaunch's Talon-A2, a reusable hypersonic test vehicle. In April of 2026, the company reported that Hadley had completed ten successful flights, including missions at sustained hypersonic speeds. So the company does have a track record of hypersonic flight, just with a different engine and a different vehicle.

Putting it all together, the latest AFRL funding supports more than a single, isolated engine project. It advances a propulsion approach that Ursa Major hopes to apply across test vehicles and, eventually, real weapons.

But let's close with the reality check the article offers. The ten point nine million dollar award is a development milestone. Neither Ursa Major nor AFRL has publicly disclosed a schedule for fielding an operational, Draper-powered weapon. And this latest announcement does not establish that HAVOC is ready for deployment. What it does show is that the Air Force sees enough promise in a storable, throttleable, restartable rocket engine to keep paying to develop it, after two flights that reached supersonic speed.

That's the story: a room-temperature-fueled rocket engine that can throttle and restart, two supersonic demonstrator flights under its belt, and fresh Air Force funding to push it further toward the hypersonic future.

This has been US Air Force advances restartable hypersonic rocket engine to power high-speed weapons, from Interesting Engineering.

Source: https://interestingengineering.com/military/ursa-major-air-force-hypersonic-engine

US Air Force advances restartable hypersonic rocket engine to power high-speed weapons. From Interesting Engineering, by Kaif Shaikh, published November 13th, 2026.

Here's the headline in one sentence: the Air Force Research Laboratory, known as AFRL, has put more money behind a rocket engine called Draper, built by the American propulsion company Ursa Major. The engine is designed for hypersonic applications, and it has already powered two flights of an experimental missile demonstrator. Let's walk through what was announced, what makes this engine different, and just as importantly, what this news does not mean.

First, the money. AFRL has exercised a contract option worth ten point nine million dollars to keep developing the Draper engine. An option, in government contracting terms, is a pre-negotiated extension that the customer can choose to trigger. In other words, the Air Force liked what it saw and decided to keep going. This award builds on a larger, twenty-eight point six million dollar AFRL contract that was announced back in May of 2025. Under that original deal, Ursa Major was tasked with maturing the engine and integrating it into a flight demonstrator.

That demonstrator is called the Affordable Rapid Missile Demonstrator, or ARMD for short. And it uses Draper as its propulsion system. AFRL and Ursa Major first announced a flight demonstration in March of 2026, and they reported that the vehicle reached supersonic speeds. Then, roughly forty-five days later, a follow-on flight took place. That second flight expanded the demonstrator's flight envelope, meaning it pushed into new combinations of speed, altitude, and maneuvering, and it tested how the engine performed and how well it could be controlled during different phases of flight.

Now, here's an important caveat that the article is careful to make. These flights are a real development milestone, but they are not a publicly confirmed hypersonic flight. AFRL described the March demonstration as supersonic. Supersonic means faster than the speed of sound. Hypersonic is a much higher bar, generally considered to be five times the speed of sound or more. So the program's broader objective is to develop propulsion technology for future high-speed weapons and test vehicles, but what has been publicly shown so far is supersonic flight.

So why is the Air Force interested in this particular engine? It comes down to a trade-off that has shaped missile design for decades: solid rockets versus liquid rockets.

Solid rocket motors are the workhorses of most missiles. Their big advantage is that they're simple and ready to go. The fuel is cast into the motor, it sits there, and when you need it, you light it. The downside is that once a solid motor is ignited, it generally burns at a predetermined rate until it's done. You can't really turn it down, and you can't turn it off and back on.

Liquid rocket engines, on the other hand, offer much more control. You can adjust the flow of propellant, which changes the thrust. But many liquid engines use cryogenic propellants, like liquid oxygen, which have to be kept extremely cold. That means specialized temperature-controlled storage and fueling right before launch, which is not very practical for a weapon that might need to sit on a shelf, or under an aircraft wing, ready at a moment's notice.

Draper is designed to get the best of both worlds. According to Ursa Major, the engine produces about four thousand pounds of thrust, and it runs on hydrogen peroxide and kerosene in what the company calls a closed catalyst cycle. The key point is that both of those propellants can be stored at room temperature. The company says they can remain stored for years. That means a vehicle could be prepared for launch without first having to load or condition its fuel, much like a solid rocket.

But unlike a solid rocket, Draper is throttleable, meaning its thrust can be adjusted up or down during flight. And according to the company, it can also restart multiple times. Picture a missile that can burn hard to accelerate, then throttle back or shut down to coast, and then reignite later in its flight to sprint or maneuver. That kind of flexibility gives designers far more control over a vehicle's flight profile than a conventional solid motor allows.

Why does that matter? The article points to two uses. One is hypersonic test vehicles. The military needs targets and test articles that can reproduce the changing speed and maneuverability of advanced threats, the kind of hypersonic weapons that adversaries are developing. An engine that can throttle and restart can mimic those behaviors more realistically. The second use is future tactical weapons that need more control over their propulsion during flight.

The ARMD program itself is also about speed of development, not just speed of flight. It's intended to demonstrate how quickly a new propulsion system and a missile-like vehicle can be developed, integrated, and flown. Ursa Major says the first ARMD flight came about eight months after the contract began. And the second flight, coming about a month and a half after the first, showed a rapid turnaround between missions. In a defense world where programs can take a decade or more, that pace is a big part of the pitch.

Draper is also central to Ursa Major's broader hypersonics business. In February of 2026, the company unveiled a missile system called HAVOC, which it describes as a medium-range hypersonic weapon powered by the Draper engine. The company says HAVOC can throttle and restart during different phases of flight, and that it's designed for potential launch from aircraft, ships, and ground-based systems. The article is careful to note that these are company-stated design capabilities. They are not evidence that the weapon has entered operational service.

Ursa Major has another engine in its stable as well, called Hadley. Hadley is also a liquid rocket engine, and it has powered Stratolaunch's Talon-A2, a reusable hypersonic test vehicle. In April of 2026, the company reported that Hadley had completed ten successful flights, including missions at sustained hypersonic speeds. So the company does have a track record of hypersonic flight, just with a different engine and a different vehicle.

Putting it all together, the latest AFRL funding supports more than a single, isolated engine project. It advances a propulsion approach that Ursa Major hopes to apply across test vehicles and, eventually, real weapons.

But let's close with the reality check the article offers. The ten point nine million dollar award is a development milestone. Neither Ursa Major nor AFRL has publicly disclosed a schedule for fielding an operational, Draper-powered weapon. And this latest announcement does not establish that HAVOC is ready for deployment. What it does show is that the Air Force sees enough promise in a storable, throttleable, restartable rocket engine to keep paying to develop it, after two flights that reached supersonic speed.

That's the story: a room-temperature-fueled rocket engine that can throttle and restart, two supersonic demonstrator flights under its belt, and fresh Air Force funding to push it further toward the hypersonic future.

This has been US Air Force advances restartable hypersonic rocket engine to power high-speed weapons, from Interesting Engineering.

Source: https://interestingengineering.com/military/ursa-major-air-force-hypersonic-engine

item.title: Unstable plasma heats itself with waves it generates
item.description:
Unstable plasma heats itself with waves it generates, experiments reveal. This story comes from Phys.org, published November 13th, 2026, based on a release from Japan's National Institutes of Natural Sciences.

Let's start with the big picture. Fusion power is one of the great hopes for clean energy. A fusion plant would generate electricity without emitting carbon dioxide. The leading approach is to take a gas of charged particles, called a plasma, heat it to extraordinarily high temperatures, and hold it in place with powerful magnetic fields so it never touches the walls of the machine.

Getting a plasma that hot is hard. To start a fusion reaction, engineers have to pump energy in from the outside, by injecting high-energy particle beams or electromagnetic waves. That outside heating is expensive and power-hungry.

The dream is something called self-heating. Once fusion reactions begin, they produce high-energy particles. Those particles then deposit their energy back into the plasma, keeping it hot. If self-heating works well enough, operators can turn down the external heating and the plasma largely sustains its own temperature. That is the point where a fusion reactor starts to look like a real power source rather than an energy sink.

The catch is that self-heating is a complicated chain of processes. Demonstrating the whole thing requires an enormous machine, like ITER, the international fusion project under construction in France. A full demonstration of self-heating there is expected around 2040. That is a long time to wait to understand the physics.

But here's the clever part. Some individual links in that chain can be studied today, on existing machines. One of the key links is this: when a plasma becomes unstable, it generates waves. Do those waves drain energy from the plasma, or can they actually heat it?

That is the question a team at Japan's National Institute for Fusion Science set out to answer, using a machine called the Large Helical Device, or LHD. Their results were published in the journal Communications Physics.

Now, for decades, the conventional wisdom has been that plasma instability is bad news. When a plasma goes unstable and throws off waves, the thinking went, it loses energy and its temperature drops. So a huge amount of fusion research has been devoted to suppressing instabilities, keeping the plasma calm and well-behaved.

The research group, led by Professor Katsumi Ida, took a different approach. Instead of asking how to stop instability, they asked whether it might be more important to watch unstable plasma closely and figure out what it actually does. So they deliberately created unstable plasma in the LHD, and then examined it in fine detail.

To understand what they found, it helps to know about something physicists call the distribution function. Think of it as a portrait of how all the particles in the plasma are moving. Some are slow, some are fast, and the distribution function describes how many particles are moving at each speed and in which direction. Temperature, in this picture, is related to how spread out those speeds are. A wider spread of particle motion means a hotter plasma.

Scientists already knew that when an instability generates waves, it creates a temporary distortion in this distribution function. The particle motions get bunched up or skewed in an unusual way for a short time. What nobody had pinned down was what happens to the plasma's temperature after that distortion fades away.

So the team tracked the distribution function carefully through the whole episode. And here is the surprise. After the wave-driven distortion relaxed back to normal, the spread of particle motion was wider than before. In other words, the plasma had gotten hotter.

The researchers summarize the sequence like this. First, the plasma becomes unstable. Second, the instability generates waves. Third, those waves distort the distribution of particle motion. And fourth, as the distortion resolves, the distribution spreads out, meaning the plasma has been heated.

That overturns a piece of long-held intuition. Waves generated by instabilities don't only cause the plasma to lose energy. They can also put energy back in, heating the plasma itself. In this experiment, the plasma was effectively heating itself with waves it generated on its own.

Why does this matter? Because this process, waves from instabilities heating the plasma, is one of the core mechanisms underpinning self-heating in a burning fusion plasma. No machine today can demonstrate the entire self-heating process. But showing one essential piece of it experimentally, years before ITER is ready, gives researchers a much better handle on how a fusion plasma might hold onto its high temperature. It also offers a fresh perspective on instabilities. Rather than treating them purely as enemies to be stamped out, scientists may need to understand when they help.

There's a second, broader angle too. This kind of wave-driven self-heating isn't unique to fusion machines. It's described as a universal physical process that also happens in the plasma of Earth's magnetosphere, the region of space shaped by our planet's magnetic field. So the findings build a bridge between two research communities that usually work separately: fusion scientists and space plasma physicists. The team expects the result to encourage more interdisciplinary work between those fields.

So, the key takeaways. One: fusion power depends on self-heating, where the plasma keeps itself hot, but full demonstrations won't come until around 2040. Two: researchers at Japan's National Institute for Fusion Science deliberately created unstable plasma in the Large Helical Device rather than suppressing it. Three: they found that waves generated by the instability, after temporarily distorting particle motion, left the plasma hotter than before. Four: that challenges the old assumption that instabilities only drain energy, and it confirms one key building block of fusion self-heating today. And five: the same physics shows up in Earth's magnetosphere, linking fusion and space research.

The paper is by Katsumi Ida and colleagues, titled Direct observation of phase-space dynamics during energetic-particle-driven MHD bursts, published in Communications Physics in 2026. That's the story. Thanks for listening.

Source: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-unstable-plasma-generates-reveal.html

Author: National Institutes of Natural Sciences, via Phys.org

item.title: Robots to assemble solar panels in two minutes for 457 MW US project
item.description:
Robots to assemble solar panels in two minutes for a 457 megawatt US project. This one comes from Interesting Engineering, written by Muskan Bhatia and published November thirteenth, 2026.

Here is the headline idea. A large solar farm being built in Navarro County, Texas, is turning to robots to put its panels together. The project is called Tormes Solar, and when it's finished it will have a capacity of 457 megawatts. The developer is Matrix Renewables, a Spanish company, and the robotic system comes from a US company called Terabase Energy. Their platform is called Terafab V2.

So what exactly is Terafab V2? The easiest way to picture it is as a small, portable factory that gets set up right on the construction site. Terabase describes it as a modular factory. Instead of crews assembling solar hardware piece by piece out in the field, the parts are brought to this on-site production line, where robots do much of the assembly. And interestingly, the system isn't just hardware. It also helps manage and plan the whole construction project, which we'll come back to in a minute.

The upgraded version, V2, launched this past April. According to Terabase, once it's up and running continuously, it can assemble one unit in about two minutes. At that pace, the company says, it can turn out about twenty megawatts of solar capacity in a single week. The system has been field tested, and right now it's optimized for one specific combination of equipment: First Solar's Series 7 modules, and trackers made by Nextpower.

Let's talk about why anyone would want to do this. Building a utility-scale solar farm is a lot of repetitive, physical labor. It's time consuming, it's expensive, and moving bulky materials around a huge site adds even more cost. Terabase's answer is to bring the production line to the farm and automate it.

Here's how the process works, step by step. First, the raw materials get delivered to the site. That means the solar panels themselves, plus the metal hardware: frames, brackets, mounts, and long steel pieces called tracker torque tubes. Those torque tubes are the backbone of a solar tracker. They're long rotating steel tubes that let the panels tilt and follow the sun across the sky during the day.

Next, the robots go to work. They fasten the photovoltaic modules onto those torque tubes, building up finished assemblies. Then comes quality control. The system uses AI-assisted tools to check that everything has been placed and attached correctly.

After that, autonomous vehicles, which the company calls rovers, pick up the finished assemblies and carry them out across the solar farm to where they'll be installed. And finally, there's still a human step at the end. Workers in the field take the assembled units off the rovers and set them onto tracker supports that have already been fixed into the ground.

One of the selling points is how mobile all of this is. Terabase says one of these modular robotic systems can be set up in roughly four hours. That means it can be deployed quickly, and it can also be picked up and moved to a new spot on the site as construction progresses across what can be a very large piece of land. And you're not limited to one. A single project can run multiple assembly line modules at the same time to increase overall output.

Now, back to that software side. Terabase emphasizes that it isn't just dropping robots onto a field. The platform combines the automation hardware with software for planning, tracking materials, and handling logistics. It also includes a digital replica of the construction site, sometimes called a digital twin. That gives project managers a live view of what's happening, so they can monitor progress and coordinate the work more effectively.

What kind of improvement are we talking about? Terabase claims that compared with conventional methods for installing utility-scale solar, its automated approach can double labor productivity. But the company adds an important caveat: actual results depend on how the project is configured, how fully the equipment is used, and the conditions at the particular site. So, doubling is the company's own claim, and real-world mileage will vary.

There's also some track record here. The first-generation Terafab platform has been available since 2022. Terabase says it's been used to install about 40 megawatts of tracker-mounted solar capacity across several US projects, including sites in Arizona and Texas. Worth putting that in perspective: 40 megawatts total from the first generation, versus a 457 megawatt project now, and a claimed pace of 20 megawatts a week for the new version. This Texas deployment is a significant step up in scale.

Looking ahead, Terabase has two main goals. One is to make the system work with more kinds of solar modules and trackers, beyond the First Solar and Nextpower combination it's tuned for today. The other is to automate that last manual step. Remember, workers still have to lift the assembled units onto the tracker supports in the ground. The company is developing additional robots to handle that final installation step too.

So, to sum it up. A 457 megawatt solar farm in Texas is using Terabase Energy's Terafab V2, a portable robotic factory that assembles solar units on site in about two minutes each, checks them with AI-assisted tools, and sends them out on autonomous rovers for installation. It sets up in about four hours, can be moved around the site, and pairs the robots with planning software and a digital model of the project. The company claims it can produce twenty megawatts a week and double labor productivity, though it notes results depend on the site. Humans still handle the final placement for now, but Terabase is working on robots for that as well. That's the story from Interesting Engineering.

Source: https://interestingengineering.com/energy/texas-solar-farm-deploys-robots
