item.title: Quantum Computing Inc Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for Quantum Computing Incorporated, ticker Q-U-B-T, often called Q.C.I. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. The company released the numbers on Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call that afternoon. On the call were David Moskowitz, head of investor relations; Yuping Huang, chairman and chief executive officer; and Christopher Bruce Roberts, chief financial officer.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's press release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's next-day reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the lack of formal guidance, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. Revenue jumped, and the loss per share missed. Quantum Computing Incorporated generated nine point five million dollars of third-quarter revenue, compared with three hundred eighty-four thousand dollars a year earlier. That figure also exceeded the nine point two million dollars of revenue the company reported for the entire first half of twenty twenty-six. It beat published estimates. MarketBeat put the consensus at seven point six one million dollars. So this was a clear top-line beat, and a sharp step-up from the company's own recent run rate.

The bottom line went the other way. The company reported a net loss of fifteen point one million dollars, or seven cents a share, compared with net income of two point four million dollars, or one cent a share, a year earlier. MarketBeat said that missed a consensus loss of four cents by three cents. Coverage after the call treated the quarter as a revenue beat and an earnings miss, and the shares gapped down the next session. MarketBeat said the stock opened at six dollars and forty-seven cents, after a prior close of six dollars and eighty-six cents.

The company did not issue formal financial guidance. Roberts was explicit about why. He said the timing of orders and deliveries is difficult to predict, so quarter-to-quarter results are likely to be lumpy, and that the company is not giving guidance at this time. He also said that, over a twelve- to fifteen-month view, management is confident it will have a strong finish to this year and a solid backlog leading into twenty twenty-seven.

Most of the revenue growth came from businesses acquired in the first half of the year. The press release said growth was primarily driven by Luminar Semiconductors, NuCrypt, and NHanced Semiconductors, including photonic components, quantum communications products, and advanced packaging services sold to aerospace, government, and industrial customers. Huang's message was that Q.C.I. is shifting from years of building photonic-based quantum technology to putting those technologies into customers' hands and building a business that can grow sustainably. He said the company has spent years building technology designed for the real world, and that attention is now shifting from what it can build to what it can put to work for customers. That means delivering on commitments and building a business that can grow sustainably. Execution, he said, matters more than ever, and the third-quarter results, in his view, reflect progress in that direction.

Before questions, he came back to a more cautious industry point. He said quantum technology offers tremendous potential, but it is a young industry, and adoption will develop differently across markets and applications. Some customers need photonic technologies today, while others are still exploring what quantum systems can enable as they become more capable and practical. The company, he said, needs to understand those differences and be thoughtful about where it invests. As Roberts outlined, the financial position gives considerable flexibility, particularly in an industry where technology takes time to mature. For Q.C.I., that means advancing the science while building products customers can depend on, growing commercial relationships, improving manufacturing, following through on the roadmap, and being ambitious about what can be achieved while remaining realistic about what it takes to get there.

Gross profit was only four hundred twenty-eight thousand dollars, for a gross margin of four point five percent. That is a thin margin, and management did not pretend otherwise. Roberts said margins remain modest, and that as revenue grows the company sees opportunities to improve manufacturing utilization, increase operating efficiency, and expand margins over time. The company is still in the early innings of integrating acquired factories and filling them.

Operating expenses were twenty-nine point zero million dollars, compared with ten point five million dollars a year earlier. The increase was largely due to higher personnel and related costs from expanded research and development, sales, and marketing, plus about one million dollars of acquisition-related expenses. Interest and other income totaled thirteen point zero million dollars, up from three point five million dollars, mainly from interest on a much larger cash and investment balance. That interest income is a big reason the net loss was not even wider. The press release and the call both make clear that the change from year-ago net income to this quarter's net loss was due largely to higher operating expenses and to smaller mark-to-market gains on a warrant derivative, partly offset by higher revenue and higher interest income.

The balance sheet is the feature that lets the company talk about scale before the margins are healthy. Roberts said Q.C.I. ended the third quarter with approximately one point three billion dollars in cash equivalents and investments, consistent with the end of the second quarter. Total assets were about one point six billion dollars. Total liabilities were forty-seven point seven million dollars. Cash and cash equivalents were one hundred seventy-four point three million dollars, with about one point one billion dollars in investments, and working capital of about nine hundred sixteen point nine million dollars. Management said that liquidity is sufficient to fund operations for at least the next twelve months. Headcount was three hundred thirty employees, up from about three hundred ten at the end of the second quarter.

Contract backlog was thirty-nine point one million dollars, down about two million to three million dollars from the prior quarter, which Roberts attributed to the ordinary difference between contracted orders and recognized revenue. He said backlog typically burns off over twelve to eighteen months, with most of it likely to convert in the next twelve months, but with some more complex products taking longer. That timing variability is also why the company is not guiding quarter by quarter. A backlog that is only about four times this quarter's revenue, and that already declined a little as revenue was recognized, is useful, but it is not a multi-year locked-in book of business. New orders have to keep arriving for the growth to continue.

The first-half comparison is the cleanest way to see the step-up. The company did more revenue in this one quarter than in the first six months of the year combined. That is encouraging, and it is also why a single lumpy quarter should not be extrapolated in a straight line. If a few large aerospace or government deliveries slipped from the third quarter into the fourth, or the other way around, the year could still finish strong, as management expects, without every quarter looking like this one.

On the product side, Huang and the prepared materials emphasized Dirac-three, the company's quantum optimization machine. Capacity was cited at nine thousand nine hundred eighty variables, an increase from previous generations, and the first customer shipment is expected in the fourth quarter of twenty twenty-six. That shipment is one of the few dated product milestones on the call, and it is a useful checkpoint for whether the quantum story is starting to sit beside the acquired photonics revenue, or still mostly behind it. About seventy percent of current revenue is from aerospace and government subcontracts, with a long-term goal of a fifty-fifty commercial split. Getting to that split would require either a lot more commercial work, a change in the government mix, or both, and it will not happen in a single quarter.

The company also pointed to a first pharmaceutical-market collaboration with INmune Bio, a framework agreement with Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Qatar for cloud access to Dirac-three and quantum education, and a benchmark of Dirac-three against the Hexaly classical solver in which management said the quantum system showed better overall performance in time to solution and quality for specific problems. Those are management-reported comparisons and early commercial beachheads, not an independent bake-off I can certify, and not yet a second revenue engine on the scale of the acquired aerospace and government work. They do, however, show how management wants the story to broaden: from components and packaging sold mainly into government supply chains, toward quantum systems and services in new verticals, including pharma and international education and cloud access.

The manufacturing map underneath all of that is still messy, in a way the company itself admits. Eleven facilities in eight states is a lot of footprint for a company that just reported nine point five million dollars of quarterly revenue. The acquisitions were designed to bring in photonics, quantum communications, and advanced packaging, and to speed the Fab Two plan. The test now is whether that footprint gets used more fully, or whether it remains a collection of sites with a four point five percent blended gross margin and one million dollars of leftover acquisition costs in the quarter.

Capital allocation is now a central investor question, because the company has more than a billion dollars to put to work. Roberts said Q.C.I. has earmarked several hundred million dollars for capital expenditure, and that the investment planned for the NHanced Fab Two facility is in the ballpark of seventy million to eighty million dollars. Equipment orders have already begun, and a lot of that spend is expected between now and March thirty-first of next year. He also said the company continues to review deal flow and acquisition opportunities, while wanting enough working capital to ride through periods when raising capital would be highly dilutive. The company has already completed three acquisitions in about eight months.

Huang added that last year's original plan for Fab Two was a greenfield approach, with a later step expected perhaps at the end of twenty twenty-eight, and that the NHanced acquisition has accelerated that roadmap. He said the acquired facilities serve two purposes: supporting the quantum roadmap, including work toward heterogeneous integrated circuits that the team hopes to demonstrate in a twelve- to eighteen-month timeframe, or possibly sooner, and enabling volume production of quantum devices after more than twenty years of research.

Roberts also flagged a risk that did not get a lot of headlines but should be on the list. He said there is a possibility of export restrictions later on, and that I.T.A.R. regulations or other geopolitical factors could complicate future international sales of cutting-edge technology. He also said the bulk of sales and backlog is still domestic, with a few small overseas sales.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt opened with a question that led Roberts into the lumpiness of revenue and awards. Roberts said there is not much to read into a single-quarter backlog change, that backlog was down about two to three million dollars, and that backlog will fluctuate as the difference between contracted orders and recognized revenue. That set the tone for the rest of the call: this is a lumpy, low-volume, technically complex manufacturing business, not a smooth software subscription curve.

Max Michaelis of Lake Street Capital Markets asked what milestones to watch on commercial growth over the next twenty-four months, and what the bigger hurdles are on the manufacturing-scale side. Roberts repeated that the company is not giving guidance because order and delivery timing is hard to predict, that quarters will be lumpy, and that the signs of progress to watch are a strong finish to the year, a solid backlog into twenty twenty-seven, and evidence that a broader range of customers is validating the technology.

Scott Buck of Milan Partners asked how quickly the thirty-nine point one million dollar backlog converts, and about bringing manufacturing operations together. Roberts said the backlog typically converts over twelve to eighteen months, with most of it likely in the next twelve months and some taking longer because the company is building small numbers of very complex products, where a slip of a couple of weeks can move revenue recognition. On manufacturing, he said the company has operations in eight states and eleven facilities, and that the work is more about integrating the company than about a simple site consolidation, deferring some of the detail to Huang.

Nehal Chokshi of Northland Capital Markets also joined the queue, and Kieran McCabe of Cantor asked about the INmune Bio announcement, the first customer in pharma and biotech, and whether a new chief revenue officer signals a push into industries beyond aerospace and defense. Huang said yes, the company is looking at other industries, including biotech and pharma, and that the strategy is both to go deeper within organizations and to spread within those verticals. The Fab Two follow-up is where he explained that NHanced has accelerated a roadmap that had been a later greenfield plan.

Ed Woo of Ascendiant Capital asked how much of the pipeline is U.S. versus international, and about long-term revenue potential. Roberts said the bulk of sales, backlog, and revenue is still domestic, that the company is looking at international opportunities and has made a few small overseas sales, and that he would not over-specify a single long-term market size on the call. That answer sits next to his later comment about possible export restrictions. International expansion is an opportunity and a policy risk at the same time.

Jesse Sockler of B.T.I.G. asked the integration question most directly. He said a lot of the investment world still sees Luminar Semiconductors, NHanced, NuCrypt, and the core business as four separate businesses, and he asked what the first wave of flagship or integrated products looks like, and on what timeline. Huang said the acquired facilities support the quantum roadmap and have already made possible prototypes that could not have been built before the sites were combined. He said the team hopes to demonstrate some heterogeneous integrated circuits in twelve to eighteen months, perhaps sooner, and that after more than twenty years of quantum research the company now has to solve the scalable manufacturing challenge so it can put products into many customers' hands. Sockler's follow-up was about the capital plan for more than a billion dollars of cash. One more point on expectations, because the miss on earnings can be misread. item.title: Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light
item.description:
Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light. This story comes from Phys.org, written by Kayla Albert of Purdue University, and published November 12, 2026.

Quantum computers promise to solve certain problems far faster than today's supercomputers. But they could be even faster, and use much less energy, if their basic units of information were made from light. Those units are called qubits, and building them out of single particles of light, called photons, is the goal of a group of engineers at Purdue University.

The catch is that the chips needed to make photons work as qubits are hard to build. These chips are called quantum photonic integrated circuits. Purdue researchers say they have developed possible solutions to several of the biggest problems standing in the way of building them at large scale.

First, a quick refresher. An ordinary computer works with bits, and each bit is either a zero or a one. A qubit is the quantum version. Through a phenomenon called superposition, a qubit can represent zero and one at the same time, which vastly expands how much information can be processed.

So why use photons? Photons are the smallest possible particles of light, and they have real advantages. Qubits made from single photons would move through the gates of a circuit at the speed of light, moving data faster and cutting delays when an algorithm runs. Photons are also not easily disturbed by heat or other changes in their surroundings, so they can stay stable at room temperature. Many other kinds of qubits need to be kept extremely cold, which takes a lot of energy.

The problem is scale. Today's quantum photonic chips can handle only a small number of qubits. Practical calculations would need hundreds, if not thousands, of them, and that's not yet possible with these chips.

Vladimir Shalaev, the Bob and Anne Burnett Distinguished Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering at Purdue, put it this way: "Single photons are the building blocks of quantum photonics. The biggest challenges in scaling up a quantum photonic integrated circuit have to do with creating good single-photon sources."

Shalaev leads this work together with Alexandra Boltasseva, the Ron and Dotty Garvin Tonjes Distinguished Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering. Their work spans Purdue's Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, the Birck Nanotechnology Center, and the Purdue Quantum Science and Engineering Institute. Both are well known for foundational work on controlling light at the nanoscale. Both have repeatedly been named Clarivate Highly Cited Researchers, meaning their work ranks in the top one percent of citations. Boltasseva was also named to last year's Quantum 100 list, during the United Nations-designated International Year of Quantum Science and Technology.

The article describes three advances. Let's take them one at a time.

The first is a more reliable way to produce single photons.

To act as a qubit, a photon has to be generated one at a time. That sounds simple, but it's hard. In 2021, Shalaev and Boltasseva published a study in Science Advances showing a way to emit single photons using silicon nitride. That material has become the industry standard for building quantum photonic platforms.

The method the industry has typically used to produce photons is called spontaneous parametric down-conversion. The trouble is that it produces single photons inconsistently and with low efficiency.

The Purdue team's approach is different. It emits exactly one photon, at room temperature, from dozens of locations on a silicon nitride platform, every time a laser beam passes through. The photons come from tiny changes in the material's atomic structure, called defects, which the researchers deliberately create. These defects limit the light emission to one photon at a time.

Then, at the 2022 Conference on Lasers and Electro-Optics, the team showed they could control where these defects go, and how many there are, by embedding them in nanoscale pillars on the silicon nitride. That matters because it would let the platform be manufactured more uniformly, which is essential for a real chip.

The second advance is a switch that works with a single photon.

Here's the problem. Single photons don't readily interact with each other. That makes them hard to control on a chip. In a normal computer, transistors act as switches that flip bits between zero and one. A quantum photonic chip would need switches too, so that photons can act as qubits.

Last year, in a paper in Nature Nanotechnology, the Purdue team reported a switch that operates at the level of single photons.

It builds on a mechanism the industry already uses, for example in fiber-optic communications, where one light beam is used to modulate another. That mechanism is called optical nonlinearity. A "control" beam interacts with a "probe" beam. But normally that requires power levels far too high to work with single photons.

In the Purdue method, a single photon from the control beam strikes silicon and creates an electron. That electron triggers an avalanche of more electrons. The avalanche changes how light passes through the material, specifically its refractive index, the property that governs how light travels. By changing silicon's refractive index, the device lets the probe beam pass through only when a single photon has kicked off that avalanche. In effect, one photon switches a much more powerful beam on and off.

In the lab, the researchers demonstrated this by shooting two lasers through a spatial filter onto a commercial device called a single-photon avalanche diode. That let a single photon from one beam switch another, stronger beam on and off. It's the kind of switch a quantum photonic chip would need to process information.

The third advance is a tool for predicting something called quantum decoherence.

Even though photon-based qubits are less affected by their surroundings, a single disturbance can still knock a qubit out of superposition or entanglement. That introduces errors into a quantum computer's calculations. This disturbance is called decoherence.

Purdue electrical and computer engineering professor Alexander Kildishev and graduate student Pranshu Maan led a team, including Shalaev and Boltasseva, that showed a way to anticipate decoherence before it happens. They published their findings in Nature Communications in May of this year, in a paper titled "Anticipating decoherence in quantum systems."

Boltasseva explained: "Decoherence is seemingly random, but in fact there is a certain pattern that can be recognized. This study takes an important step in identifying such a pattern using machine learning."

Using statistical-physics analysis, the team found that decoherence unfolds over time in a pattern. They then used machine learning to confirm that these patterns contain information that can be predicted. They combined these pieces into a framework that learns the behavior of a quantum system, so that decoherence could be controlled proactively, rather than only dealt with after it happens.

They focused on one major cause of decoherence, called spectral diffusion. That's when an emitted photon drifts across the electromagnetic spectrum because of natural disorder in its surroundings. Its frequency shifts, and so does its energy. Superposition only works if all the photons in a quantum system are indistinguishable from one another. So if a single photon's energy changes, superposition can fall apart.

The researchers discovered that these spectral shifts carry a kind of memory. The way a photon's frequency has wandered in the past reveals a predictable pattern over time. So the team built an algorithm with a built-in memory mechanism and trained it on data from individual quantum emitters to predict future shifts. Using those predictions, they showed that an anticipatory control approach could reduce spectral shifts by as much as twenty-fold in the systems they studied.

Why does that matter so much? Shalaev explained it with an example. "You can't get rid of decoherence, it's the law of nature that everything fluctuates. But if you recognize the pattern of decoherence and learn how to control it, then you can minimize it."

He continued: "Let's say you need a hundred qubits to run a quantum algorithm, but typically far more than that, say 10,000 qubits, to deal with errors caused by decoherence. If I minimize those errors somehow, then the number of qubits needed to run my algorithm would also be minimized."

In other words, simply being able to predict decoherence could dramatically cut the number of qubits a useful quantum computer needs.

In principle, this approach could lay the groundwork for anticipating decoherence across many quantum systems at once, which is what a scalable quantum computer would require. Those predictions could be paired with active tuning to keep different photon emitters closely aligned, making the photons they produce more indistinguishable and better synchronized.

What's next? The team plans to use tools from statistical physics to pull out hidden properties of a quantum system's fluctuating environment from its measured behavior. They'll feed those physical insights into their machine-learning models to make them better at predicting decoherence. They also want to see whether the models can pinpoint the microscopic processes that cause spectral shifts. The long-term goal is to predict and suppress decoherence before it seriously disrupts the quantum state.

So, to sum up. Purdue engineers are working on three key pieces of a light-based quantum computer: a dependable, room-temperature source that emits exactly one photon at a time; a switch that a single photon can flip; and a machine-learning tool that predicts decoherence before it happens, cutting one major source of error by up to twenty times. None of this is a finished quantum computer. But each piece tackles a real obstacle to building photonic quantum chips at the scale needed for practical work.

That was "Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light," from Phys.org and Purdue University.

Source: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-advances-quantum-harnesses.html

item.title: D-Wave Quantum Q3 2026 Earnings Brief
item.description:
Welcome to this earnings brief for D-Wave Quantum, ticker Q-B-T-S. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. D-Wave released the numbers on Tuesday, November tenth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call the same day. On the call were Alan Baratz, chief executive officer; Greg Golkov, acting chief financial officer; and Kevin Hunt, senior director of investor relations.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's official earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the lack of numerical guidance, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. Revenue beat, earnings missed, bookings were lumpy, and the cash burn rose. Third-quarter revenue was four point five million dollars, up twenty-one percent from a year earlier. Yahoo Finance and other recaps said that was about fourteen percent above consensus, so this was a top-line beat. The loss was wider than estimates. G.A.A.P. net loss was forty-eight point two million dollars, or thirteen cents a share, compared with a loss of one hundred thirty-nine point nine million dollars, or about forty-one cents, a year earlier. The year-over-year improvement is not an operating miracle. Golkov said it was due primarily to a one hundred twenty-two million dollar decrease in non-cash charges related to the remeasurement of warrant liabilities in twenty twenty-five, after the remaining publicly traded warrants were redeemed in November twenty twenty-five. Adjusted earnings measures still missed. Recaps said G.A.A.P. earnings missed a consensus loss of about ten cents, and that an adjusted loss of about eleven cents also missed a ten-cent consensus. Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss was thirty-seven point seven million dollars, widening by seventeen million dollars year over year, as the company spent more on product development and go-to-market work.

The bookings story depends on the time window you pick. Bookings for the first nine months were thirty-seven point four million dollars, up six hundred eleven percent from a year earlier, and that figure includes a twenty million dollar system sale to Florida Atlantic University. Third-quarter bookings, though, were only one point nine million dollars, down nineteen percent year over year, because of the timing of large transactions. Golkov was explicit that bookings in any single quarter can vary significantly based on that timing. Remaining performance obligations, or R.P.O., were thirty-eight point three million dollars, up one thousand two hundred twenty-one percent from two point nine million dollars a year earlier. He said fifty-nine percent of that balance is expected to be recognized as revenue within twelve months after September thirtieth, and seventy-one percent over the twenty-four months following that date. The sales pipeline's dollar value increased more than seventy-five percent from the end of the second quarter, and has more than tripled since the end of twenty twenty-five, driven by interest in system sales.

The company does not provide numerical revenue guidance. Baratz said so directly when asked about twenty twenty-seven. What he would say is that he expects system sales, quantum compute as a service, professional services, and partner sales all to grow in twenty twenty-seven over what the company expects by the end of twenty twenty-six. The near-term revenue watch item is more specific. Golkov said D-Wave expects to deliver the Florida Atlantic University system in the fourth quarter and to recognize a substantial portion of the related revenue then, with an additional portion recognized over the installation period, typically several months after delivery, which in that case would likely be early twenty twenty-seven, plus smaller recurring streams for maintenance and cloud access over several years. If that delivery happens on that schedule, the fourth quarter should be much larger than the third. If it slips, the lumpy pattern continues.

The revenue mix is shifting toward services and enterprise work, which helped growth and hurt margin. Subscription revenue from the Leap cloud service, sometimes described as quantum compute as a service, was two point two million dollars, up fifty-six percent year over year. Professional services revenue was two point zero million dollars, up three hundred eighteen percent, helped by a Fortune one hundred engagement and gate-model research projects. System sales and other revenue were only three hundred sixty thousand dollars, down one point five million dollars year over year because of delivery timing. Commercial revenue was fifty-two percent of the total, up from thirty-one percent a year earlier. G.A.A.P. gross margin fell to fifty-two point nine percent from seventy-one point four percent, and non-G.A.A.P. gross margin was sixty-three point six percent, down fourteen point one points, primarily because professional services carry a lower margin than the mix a year ago.

Costs rose sharply. G.A.A.P. operating expenses were fifty-five point nine million dollars on the call, up eighty-four percent, or twenty-five point five million dollars, from a year earlier. Golkov broke that increase into twelve point three million dollars of personnel costs, four point one million dollars of stock-based compensation, four point six million dollars of depreciation and amortization, one point one million dollars of third-party professional fees, and one point one million dollars of marketing expenses. Non-G.A.A.P. adjusted operating expenses were forty point five million dollars, up seventy-two percent. Operating cash use for the nine months ended September thirtieth was one hundred nine million dollars, compared with fifty-three point six million dollars a year earlier. Cash and marketable securities were five hundred three point four million dollars, down forty percent year over year, primarily because of about two hundred fifty-three million dollars used to acquire Quantum Circuits in January twenty twenty-six. The company also executed a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for access to up to one hundred million dollars of CHIPS and Science Act funding, in installments upon satisfying specified milestones. No CHIPS Act funds had been received as of quarter-end.

Baratz framed D-Wave as the only dual-platform quantum company, with annealing systems in use today and fault-tolerant gate-model systems in development. On the commercial side, he said NTT DOCOMO, Japan's largest mobile operator, deployed its second production application powered by D-Wave's hybrid quantum technology, reducing daily peak location-registration signals by sixty-five point three percent and paging signals by seven point zero percent in the published example, and completing a representative optimization across three hundred thirty-three base stations in about five minutes. He also said the company continues to make progress with other large enterprise customers pursuing production applications, including UnitedHealth Group's Optum and A.T. and T. A Fortune one hundred engagement, first discussed in the first quarter, is a two-year, ten million dollar deal to pursue multiple applications, with the first already in production and others making progress. Partners are becoming more important. C.G.I., after a year of collaboration, plans to integrate D-Wave's platforms into its technology-services portfolio, with an expected focus on logistics, transportation, and retail. At a sold-out user conference in Seoul, the company also announced a memorandum of understanding with L.G. C.N.S., a technology arm of the L.G. Group, focused on enterprise optimization inside the group and among that firm's customers in South Korea and beyond. Baratz said enterprises need help identifying the right problems, developing applications, and integrating them into existing operations, and that partners who already understand those customers can expand D-Wave's reach.

Manufacturing is part of the same story. D-Wave extended its long-standing relationship with SkyWater through a multiyear agreement for semiconductor process development and manufacturing. A proof-of-technology project that used D-Wave's annealing systems to optimize maintenance schedules at SkyWater's fab reduced lot delays by up to thirty percent, according to Baratz, and that work is now advancing to a proof of concept that will add resource availability, technician constraints, and other fab-specific limits. SkyWater has been a partner for more than ten years. Baratz also said prudent supply-chain management requires diversification, so the company will continue to qualify additional manufacturing sources.

On the product side, the company announced performance gains to its Strive hybrid solver, available through the Leap cloud service. On assembly-line balancing benchmark problems, Baratz said the enhanced solver found better solutions in fifteen seconds than the previous version found in one hundred twenty seconds. He also pointed to scientific work on the annealing systems, including a preprint on analog-digital quantum computation and an October preprint describing experiments that realized topological insulators in one, two, and three dimensions using more than seven hundred qubits, which the company believes include the first programmable quantum-dynamics experiments in three dimensions.

The annealing hardware roadmap has two scaling technologies: superconducting interconnects for multichip systems, and scalable input-output control circuitry for much larger processors. Baratz said the company has already shown experimentally that it can achieve strong coupling between prototype annealing fabrics interconnected across two chips, has completed the design of a dual-chip annealing processor, and was releasing that design for fabrication in the week of the call. He also said D-Wave was on track to complete fabrication of its first scalable input-output development wafers in November. those steps are toward larger systems on the roadmap, including twenty-thousand-qubit and, ultimately, one-hundred-thousand-qubit annealing systems. The next-generation Advantage Three system, he later told analysts, is intended to be a multichip solution, scaling by interconnecting multiple processor chips rather than only by putting more qubits on a single chip.

On systems, D-Wave delivered Italy's first annealing quantum computer, a four-thousand-four-hundred-plus-qubit Advantage Two system, for installation at Villa Saporiti in Como, funded by Swiss Quantum Technology, to support Q-Alliance efforts in Europe. The company also has a multiyear semiconductor process and manufacturing agreement with SkyWater, extending a ten-year technology partnership. On the gate-model roadmap, D-Wave launched a simulator beta program in early October for error-aware programming, built around the company's dual-rail superconducting technology. Baratz said that architecture features built-in error detection, which is designed to reduce the hardware overhead required for quantum error correction. Beta participants include both commercial and research organizations, among them B.B.V.A., FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University, and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, He said the company is on track to complete a seventeen-qubit gate-model system and is already discussing seventeen-qubit system orders for delivery in twenty twenty-seven. The longer-term roadmap targets one hundred logical qubits capable of reliably executing more than one million operations by twenty thirty-two.

Baratz spent time defining what D-Wave means by a logical qubit, because, in his words, different definitions are floating around, some of them a bit misleading. He said it is generally accepted that a useful fault-tolerant system needs at least one hundred fault-tolerant logical qubits, with fault tolerance defined as the ability to perform at least one million gate operations successfully, and that the company is not aware of any quantum-computing firm that has produced even one logical qubit meeting that standard today. D-Wave's published timeline is to achieve the first fully error-corrected, fault-tolerant logical qubit by twenty twenty-eight, and then one hundred of them by twenty thirty-two. He cautioned investors to clarify other vendors' definitions, some of which, he said, are only error-detected, only partially error-corrected, or below the generally accepted fault-tolerant threshold.

The CHIPS agreement is intended to support both roadmaps: a one-hundred-thousand-qubit annealing system aimed at optimization, materials simulation, blockchain, and artificial intelligence, and a ten-thousand-qubit gate-model system designed to enable those one hundred logical qubits. Baratz also cited third-party analyst placements. He reminded listeners that I.D.C. named D-Wave as one of only two companies in the leaders category in its twenty twenty-six quantum-computing vendor assessment, and that Gartner had recognized the company as a market shaper and as one of only six vendors in the upper-right quadrant of an emerging-market quantum assessment as of November twenty twenty-six. Before handing the call to Golkov, he also recognized two board additions: Bernard Gavgani, former group chief information officer of B.N.P. Paribas, and Kevin Krysler, who joined the board and audit committee.

Golkov added that, in the third quarter, D-Wave recognized revenue from more than one hundred customers. G.A.A.P. gross profit was two point four million dollars, down three hundred thousand dollars, or eleven percent, year over year, while non-G.A.A.P. gross profit was two point nine million dollars, essentially flat. Gross margin, he said, can fluctuate significantly depending on product mix. Third-quarter bookings of one point nine million dollars were down four hundred thirty-five thousand dollars, or nineteen percent, from a year earlier, a decline he again tied to the timing of larger transactions.

Now to the question-and-answer session, from the Motley Fool transcript.

John McPeake of Rosenblatt asked about on-chip qubit-control multiplexing, a bottleneck in the superconducting camp. Baratz said D-Wave's annealing systems today can control more than four thousand qubits with two hundred to three hundred input-output lines, whereas gate-model systems typically require three to five lines per qubit. The company multiplexes control signals and then decodes and routes them on chip, and it is carrying that approach into the gate-model systems. The first chip design with the new scalable input-output control for gate-model systems was out for fabrication, and Baratz said the company expected the chip back in November to begin testing. The goal, he said, is to control one hundred logical qubits with a couple of hundred input-output lines, two hundred to three hundred, and that first returned chip will show whether the company can get there.

William Kingsley Crane of Canaccord Genuity asked about the SkyWater relationship, including intellectual-property protections and whether the partnership had been extended or expanded. Baratz said the SkyWater team had been supportive in working through an agreement that gives D-Wave confidence its intellectual property will be protected and that the skilled SkyWater people on the program will remain part of it. He also said the relationship has expanded in a different direction: D-Wave is now a supplier to SkyWater as well, after the successful proof of technology, with the work moving on to a proof of concept. Crane's follow-up was about the post-election environment and whether support for quantum programs might change. Baratz said he was not seeing any changes in the strength of the pipeline or, perhaps more important, in the sales agreements in negotiation, and that he has seen continued forward momentum.

Kevin Garrigan of Jefferies asked about supply-chain constraints, including dilution refrigerators. Baratz said lead times are longer than the company prefers, that Maybell in the United States is coming on strong and that D-Wave has ordered one of their refrigerators to qualify it, and that with more suppliers he is hopeful timelines may fall rather than lengthen. He also said that as the system-sales pipeline grows and new deals progress, the company is starting to buy ahead for some longer-lead items.

Harsh Kumar of B.M.O. asked Baratz to explain the dual-chip annealing processor and why it matters for getting to twenty thousand or one hundred thousand qubits. Baratz said the current Advantage Two processor has grown qubit count by putting more qubits on a chip, but the next-generation Advantage Three system will be a multichip solution. Two technologies are required: interconnecting processor chips while preserving superconducting and quantum properties, and keeping the number of input-output lines from growing significantly. The company has demonstrated interconnects on sample chips at a small scale and was starting fabrication of its first pair of interconnected actual annealing processor chips, which it will then test as a single integrated processor.

Gary Mobley of StoneX asked, without requesting explicit twenty twenty-seven revenue guidance, how the composition of twenty twenty-seven revenue might change, including presales of seventeen-qubit gate-model systems, partnership-driven sales such as those with C.G.I., more Leap cloud revenue, and government work. Baratz declined to give numbers or breakdowns, then said he expects all of those streams to grow in twenty twenty-seven. Because system sales are much larger bookings, and because their revenue is typically recognized over a shorter period than cloud subscriptions, he said the mix on bookings, and possibly on revenue, may become more significant for system sales. Partners, he said, are just getting started, and twenty twenty-seven is a year when that should start to come online rather than already being a large component. On government, he said D-Wave is seeing more interest from the U.S. government in annealing systems than it has ever seen, with good progress on a couple of fairly significant application opportunities he hopes to discuss in the relatively near future, and that government should become a significantly larger component than it has been.

Tyler, asking for Richard Shannon of Craig-Hallum, asked about NTT DOCOMO's applications, including how often they run and whether the customer developed them on its own or used D-Wave professional services, and also about what was driving the Strive solver's performance. Baratz said NTT DOCOMO developed both production applications on its own, after establishing a strong team, and that both are in production today. Professional services, he said, are a means to an end. The company does not really want to be a large professional-services firm. It wants to sell systems and quantum compute as a service, and it uses professional services to help customers get value from those offerings. The two DOCOMO applications, he added, run relatively infrequently, not on a daily or weekly basis, even though they can make an important operational and financial impact. Most of the Strive improvement, he said, was a rework of the code, with some additional capabilities as well.

Troy Jensen of Cantor Fitzgerald asked whether sovereign-supply-chain pressure, after a user conference in Asia, is showing up globally the way it has in North America. The question broke up at first, and Baratz asked him to repeat it. He then said the European Union, for example, has taken a strong position that E.U. quantum funding can go only to E.U. companies, and that this is starting to spill over into some countries. In Asia, he said, the company is not seeing that same hard line, but is being asked to incorporate local companies into the supply chain for some components on systems delivered there. He is not convinced the industry will ever source everything locally, because some components are simply made better elsewhere, so the supply chain will, by necessity, remain more global. Europe, he said, is a little more challenging, and if country-level money follows the E.U. path, D-Wave would look more to independent or commercial funding, as in the Italy system funded by Swiss Quantum Technology, which he said is not really a government entity.

Krish Sankar of T.D. Cowen asked how much of the one hundred million dollars of CHIPS funding can be allocated to superconducting gate technology, and also about integrating a cryogenic control chip with the annealing systems. Baratz said the first chips that implement the new cryogenic control architecture, designed to work with both annealing and gate-model systems, were due back in November, so testing was just about to begin. On the funding split, he said the work is really on how the company designs, fabricates, and tests the chips, or quantum processing units, and that this work can be applied to both roadmaps more or less equally, with some items more applicable to annealing and some to the gate-model side. An analyst named Rebecca, asking for Craig Ellis of B. Riley, said the R.P.O. conversion commentary implied a strong revenue ramp and asked what is in the pipeline and what would need to close to meet or exceed that pace. Baratz would not discuss deals in flight. Golkov said the R.P.O. balance has grown because of system-sales opportunities and the Fortune one hundred enterprise deal, and then repeated the fifty-nine percent and seventy-one percent conversion timelines.

Shadi Mitwalli, asking for Quinn Bolton of Needham, asked whether discussions around seventeen-qubit system sales are with existing or new customers. Baratz said discussions are with both existing and new customers. The follow-up was about the unnamed Fortune one hundred professional-services customer: how long D-Wave has been engaged, and what sector applications they are targeting. Baratz said this was the first two-year, ten million dollar deal to pursue multiple applications, that the first is already in production, that several others are making good progress and are expected to move into production in the not-too-distant future, and that a lot of the quarter's professional-services work supported that engagement.

The stock fell after the report. TipRanks said D-Wave dropped eight point six percent, closing at ten dollars and forty-eight cents, after the earnings miss and the nineteen percent decline in third-quarter bookings. That is a next-session snapshot from published coverage, not a complete trading history, but the direction matches a quarter in which revenue beat and the loss, the cash burn, and the weak quarterly bookings print were the sour notes.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether the Florida Atlantic University system is delivered in the fourth quarter and whether a substantial portion of that twenty million dollar sale is recognized on the expected schedule, with the rest in early twenty twenty-seven.

Second, whether the thirty-eight point three million dollars of remaining performance obligations converts at the fifty-nine percent twelve-month and seventy-one percent twenty-four-month pace Golkov described, and whether the seventy-five percent pipeline increase turns into bookings after a one point nine million dollar bookings quarter.

Third, cash use. Nine-month operating cash use of one hundred nine million dollars, a five hundred three point four million dollar cash and securities balance after the Quantum Circuits acquisition, and a still-undrawn CHIPS award of up to one hundred million dollars are the funding facts.

Fourth, mix and margin. Professional services helped growth and cut gross margin. If system sales rebound in the fourth quarter, the mix should improve. If services remain the growth engine, margins may stay lower.

Fifth, the seventeen-qubit gate-model system, discussions of twenty twenty-seven deliveries, and the longer path to a first fault-tolerant logical qubit by twenty twenty-eight and one hundred of them by twenty thirty-two, alongside the annealing commercial work already in production at customers such as NTT DOCOMO and the Fortune one hundred account.

Sixth, partner and government contributions, which Baratz said are early, with twenty twenty-seven as the year they should start to show up, and with more U.S. government interest in annealing than the company has seen before. Watch also whether E.U. funding limits European placements, and whether those new chips test as planned.

Let me close with a short recap.

D-Wave beat on third-quarter revenue of four point five million dollars, up twenty-one percent and above consensus, but missed on a thirteen-cent G.A.A.P. loss and a wider thirty-seven point seven million dollar adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss. Nine-month bookings jumped six hundred eleven percent, to thirty-seven point four million dollars, thanks in large part to a twenty million dollar Florida Atlantic University system sale, while third-quarter bookings fell nineteen percent to one point nine million dollars on timing. Remaining performance obligations were thirty-eight point three million dollars, and the company expects to recognize a substantial share of the university system sale in the fourth quarter. Cash and securities were five hundred three point four million dollars after a two hundred fifty-three million dollar acquisition, and no formal numerical guidance was given, though management expects all major revenue streams to grow in twenty twenty-seven. Shares fell after the report. The follow-through is the fourth-quarter delivery, the conversion of a much larger backlog, and whether the higher spending starts to show up as lasting system and production-application growth.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/10/d-wave-qbts-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/

Author: D-Wave Quantum

Welcome to this earnings brief for D-Wave Quantum, ticker Q-B-T-S. This episode covers the company's third-quarter results for twenty twenty-six. The quarter ended on September thirtieth. D-Wave released the numbers on Tuesday, November tenth, twenty twenty-six, and held its conference call the same day. On the call were Alan Baratz, chief executive officer; Greg Golkov, acting chief financial officer; and Kevin Hunt, senior director of investor relations.

This brief is based on the Motley Fool transcript of that call, the company's official earnings release, and contemporaneous coverage, including published consensus estimates and the stock's reaction. I will cover the results against expectations, the lack of numerical guidance, management's key points, notable analyst questions, and what to watch next.

Here is the headline. Revenue beat, earnings missed, bookings were lumpy, and the cash burn rose. Third-quarter revenue was four point five million dollars, up twenty-one percent from a year earlier. Yahoo Finance and other recaps said that was about fourteen percent above consensus, so this was a top-line beat. The loss was wider than estimates. G.A.A.P. net loss was forty-eight point two million dollars, or thirteen cents a share, compared with a loss of one hundred thirty-nine point nine million dollars, or about forty-one cents, a year earlier. The year-over-year improvement is not an operating miracle. Golkov said it was due primarily to a one hundred twenty-two million dollar decrease in non-cash charges related to the remeasurement of warrant liabilities in twenty twenty-five, after the remaining publicly traded warrants were redeemed in November twenty twenty-five. Adjusted earnings measures still missed. Recaps said G.A.A.P. earnings missed a consensus loss of about ten cents, and that an adjusted loss of about eleven cents also missed a ten-cent consensus. Adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss was thirty-seven point seven million dollars, widening by seventeen million dollars year over year, as the company spent more on product development and go-to-market work.

The bookings story depends on the time window you pick. Bookings for the first nine months were thirty-seven point four million dollars, up six hundred eleven percent from a year earlier, and that figure includes a twenty million dollar system sale to Florida Atlantic University. Third-quarter bookings, though, were only one point nine million dollars, down nineteen percent year over year, because of the timing of large transactions. Golkov was explicit that bookings in any single quarter can vary significantly based on that timing. Remaining performance obligations, or R.P.O., were thirty-eight point three million dollars, up one thousand two hundred twenty-one percent from two point nine million dollars a year earlier. He said fifty-nine percent of that balance is expected to be recognized as revenue within twelve months after September thirtieth, and seventy-one percent over the twenty-four months following that date. The sales pipeline's dollar value increased more than seventy-five percent from the end of the second quarter, and has more than tripled since the end of twenty twenty-five, driven by interest in system sales.

The company does not provide numerical revenue guidance. Baratz said so directly when asked about twenty twenty-seven. What he would say is that he expects system sales, quantum compute as a service, professional services, and partner sales all to grow in twenty twenty-seven over what the company expects by the end of twenty twenty-six. The near-term revenue watch item is more specific. Golkov said D-Wave expects to deliver the Florida Atlantic University system in the fourth quarter and to recognize a substantial portion of the related revenue then, with an additional portion recognized over the installation period, typically several months after delivery, which in that case would likely be early twenty twenty-seven, plus smaller recurring streams for maintenance and cloud access over several years. If that delivery happens on that schedule, the fourth quarter should be much larger than the third. If it slips, the lumpy pattern continues.

The revenue mix is shifting toward services and enterprise work, which helped growth and hurt margin. Subscription revenue from the Leap cloud service, sometimes described as quantum compute as a service, was two point two million dollars, up fifty-six percent year over year. Professional services revenue was two point zero million dollars, up three hundred eighteen percent, helped by a Fortune one hundred engagement and gate-model research projects. System sales and other revenue were only three hundred sixty thousand dollars, down one point five million dollars year over year because of delivery timing. Commercial revenue was fifty-two percent of the total, up from thirty-one percent a year earlier. G.A.A.P. gross margin fell to fifty-two point nine percent from seventy-one point four percent, and non-G.A.A.P. gross margin was sixty-three point six percent, down fourteen point one points, primarily because professional services carry a lower margin than the mix a year ago.

Costs rose sharply. G.A.A.P. operating expenses were fifty-five point nine million dollars on the call, up eighty-four percent, or twenty-five point five million dollars, from a year earlier. Golkov broke that increase into twelve point three million dollars of personnel costs, four point one million dollars of stock-based compensation, four point six million dollars of depreciation and amortization, one point one million dollars of third-party professional fees, and one point one million dollars of marketing expenses. Non-G.A.A.P. adjusted operating expenses were forty point five million dollars, up seventy-two percent. Operating cash use for the nine months ended September thirtieth was one hundred nine million dollars, compared with fifty-three point six million dollars a year earlier. Cash and marketable securities were five hundred three point four million dollars, down forty percent year over year, primarily because of about two hundred fifty-three million dollars used to acquire Quantum Circuits in January twenty twenty-six. The company also executed a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for access to up to one hundred million dollars of CHIPS and Science Act funding, in installments upon satisfying specified milestones. No CHIPS Act funds had been received as of quarter-end.

Baratz framed D-Wave as the only dual-platform quantum company, with annealing systems in use today and fault-tolerant gate-model systems in development. On the commercial side, he said NTT DOCOMO, Japan's largest mobile operator, deployed its second production application powered by D-Wave's hybrid quantum technology, reducing daily peak location-registration signals by sixty-five point three percent and paging signals by seven point zero percent in the published example, and completing a representative optimization across three hundred thirty-three base stations in about five minutes. He also said the company continues to make progress with other large enterprise customers pursuing production applications, including UnitedHealth Group's Optum and A.T. and T. A Fortune one hundred engagement, first discussed in the first quarter, is a two-year, ten million dollar deal to pursue multiple applications, with the first already in production and others making progress. Partners are becoming more important. C.G.I., after a year of collaboration, plans to integrate D-Wave's platforms into its technology-services portfolio, with an expected focus on logistics, transportation, and retail. At a sold-out user conference in Seoul, the company also announced a memorandum of understanding with L.G. C.N.S., a technology arm of the L.G. Group, focused on enterprise optimization inside the group and among that firm's customers in South Korea and beyond. Baratz said enterprises need help identifying the right problems, developing applications, and integrating them into existing operations, and that partners who already understand those customers can expand D-Wave's reach.

SkyWater has been a partner for more than ten years. On the funding split, he said the work is really on how the company designs, fabricates, and tests the chips, or quantum processing units, and that this work can be applied to both roadmaps more or less equally, with some items more applicable to annealing and some to the gate-model side. An analyst named Rebecca, asking for Craig Ellis of B. Riley, said the R.P.O. conversion commentary implied a strong revenue ramp and asked what is in the pipeline and what would need to close to meet or exceed that pace. Baratz would not discuss deals in flight. Golkov said the R.P.O. balance has grown because of system-sales opportunities and the Fortune one hundred enterprise deal, and then repeated the fifty-nine percent and seventy-one percent conversion timelines.

Shadi Mitwalli, asking for Quinn Bolton of Needham, asked whether discussions around seventeen-qubit system sales are with existing or new customers. Baratz said discussions are with both existing and new customers. The follow-up was about the unnamed Fortune one hundred professional-services customer: how long D-Wave has been engaged, and what sector applications they are targeting. Baratz said this was the first two-year, ten million dollar deal to pursue multiple applications, that the first is already in production, that several others are making good progress and are expected to move into production in the not-too-distant future, and that a lot of the quarter's professional-services work supported that engagement.

The stock fell after the report. TipRanks said D-Wave dropped eight point six percent, closing at ten dollars and forty-eight cents, after the earnings miss and the nineteen percent decline in third-quarter bookings. That is a next-session snapshot from published coverage, not a complete trading history, but the direction matches a quarter in which revenue beat and the loss, the cash burn, and the weak quarterly bookings print were the sour notes.

Here is what is fair to watch next.

First, whether the Florida Atlantic University system is delivered in the fourth quarter and whether a substantial portion of that twenty million dollar sale is recognized on the expected schedule, with the rest in early twenty twenty-seven.

Second, whether the thirty-eight point three million dollars of remaining performance obligations converts at the fifty-nine percent twelve-month and seventy-one percent twenty-four-month pace Golkov described, and whether the seventy-five percent pipeline increase turns into bookings after a one point nine million dollar bookings quarter.

Third, cash use. Nine-month operating cash use of one hundred nine million dollars, a five hundred three point four million dollar cash and securities balance after the Quantum Circuits acquisition, and a still-undrawn CHIPS award of up to one hundred million dollars are the funding facts.

Fourth, mix and margin. Professional services helped growth and cut gross margin. If system sales rebound in the fourth quarter, the mix should improve. If services remain the growth engine, margins may stay lower.

Fifth, the seventeen-qubit gate-model system, discussions of twenty twenty-seven deliveries, and the longer path to a first fault-tolerant logical qubit by twenty twenty-eight and one hundred of them by twenty thirty-two, alongside the annealing commercial work already in production at customers such as NTT DOCOMO and the Fortune one hundred account.

Sixth, partner and government contributions, which Baratz said are early, with twenty twenty-seven as the year they should start to show up, and with more U.S. government interest in annealing than the company has seen before. Watch also whether E.U. funding limits European placements, and whether those new chips test as planned.

Let me close with a short recap.

D-Wave beat on third-quarter revenue of four point five million dollars, up twenty-one percent and above consensus, but missed on a thirteen-cent G.A.A.P. loss and a wider thirty-seven point seven million dollar adjusted E.B.I.T.D.A. loss. Nine-month bookings jumped six hundred eleven percent, to thirty-seven point four million dollars, thanks in large part to a twenty million dollar Florida Atlantic University system sale, while third-quarter bookings fell nineteen percent to one point nine million dollars on timing. Remaining performance obligations were thirty-eight point three million dollars, and the company expects to recognize a substantial share of the university system sale in the fourth quarter. Cash and securities were five hundred three point four million dollars after a two hundred fifty-three million dollar acquisition, and no formal numerical guidance was given, though management expects all major revenue streams to grow in twenty twenty-seven. Shares fell after the report. The follow-through is the fourth-quarter delivery, the conversion of a much larger backlog, and whether the higher spending starts to show up as lasting system and production-application growth.

Thanks for listening.

Source: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/11/10/d-wave-qbts-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/
